true_names: MasakhaNER 1.0 and 2.0: released NER predictions | afrieval
known_results: The task prompt names MasakhaNER, and Twi is one of the languages added in MasakhaNER 2.0. Fine-tuned models such as AfroXLMR-large reach about 75–80 F1 on Twi. Zero-shot or prompted LLMs like GPT-4 score much lower, often below 50 F1 (for example, in AfroBench evaluations).

guess: Anthropic HH-RLHF red-team prompts (possibly via BeaverTails/PKU-SafeRLHF)
known_results: These are casual, multi-turn-style harmful prompts written by human red-teamers. They're used to measure harmlessness and refusal rates. Modern safety-tuned models refuse or redirect nearly all of them, and harmlessness scores are usually reported as preference-model or win-rate results.

Aider Polyglot has 225 hard Exercism exercises in C++, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python and Rust. Frontier models went from roughly 50–60% to over 80–90% pass rate (with two attempts), and reasoning models such as o3, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5 and Claude top the leaderboard.
GPT-3 scored about 44% on MMLU, and GPT-4 reached about 86%. Current frontier models score around 88–92% and have essentially saturated it, which is why harder variants such as MMLU-Pro were created.

AI2D is a multiple-choice benchmark of grade-school science diagrams. Strong multimodal models like GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Qwen2-VL score about 85–95%, while early VLMs scored much lower.

guess: BIRD (BIg Bench for LaRge-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL), dev set
known_results: Human performance on execution accuracy is about 93%. When the benchmark came out, ChatGPT scored roughly 40% and GPT-4 about 54%. Leading agentic or ensemble systems later reached about 70–77% on the test leaderboard.

Modern large models reach high accuracy on disambiguated contexts, often above 90%. On ambiguous contexts they still pick stereotype-consistent answers some of the time. Model reports such as Anthropic's and Google's publish BBQ accuracy and bias scores, and frontier models score close to the ceiling with small bias scores.

guess: AVerImaTeC (image-text claim verification, the multimodal extension of AVeriTeC)
known_results: Real-world image-text claims checked against evidence retrieved from the web, with question-answer evidence annotations. Baseline systems built on multimodal LLMs scored low when evidence and verdict had to be correct together, and they lagged well behind runs that used gold evidence.

guess: BIRD (BIg Bench for LaRge-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL), Mini-Dev / dev set
known_results: Human data engineers reach about 92.96% execution accuracy. GPT-4 started out around 46–54% EX, and the best agentic and fine-tuned systems on the leaderboard now get roughly 75–80%.

BertaQA (HiTZ, 2024) is a set of parallel English/Basque trivia questions with 3 options, split into local Basque-culture and global topics. Models do much better on global questions (often 70–90%+ for strong LLMs) than on local Basque ones, where they lag by roughly 10–30 points. Continued pretraining on Basque, as with Latxa, improves the local scores.

The items look like BeaverTails / PKU-SafeRLHF harmful prompts covering categories such as drugs, animal abuse and self-harm. Models are judged on harmlessness rates. Safety-tuned models like Alpaca-7B with Safe RLHF score much better than base models, and strong aligned chat models reach high harmless rates.

Belebele is a multiple-choice reading comprehension benchmark covering 122 language variants, built on FLORES-200 passages. Strong LLMs like GPT-4 score above 90% on English, but accuracy is much lower on low-resource African languages like Northern Sotho, roughly 50–70% for large models and close to chance for smaller ones.

ClashEval tests whether LLMs stick with their own knowledge or follow retrieved context that has been altered to be wrong. As I recall, models like GPT-4o adopted incorrect context more than 60% of the time, and Claude Opus was among the best at resisting it.

C-Eval is a Chinese multiple-choice exam suite with 52 subjects, including advanced mathematics, discrete mathematics and Chinese language. GPT-4 scored about 67-69% at release; later models such as Qwen, DeepSeek and GPT-4o-class models score in the high 80s to 90s.

CMMLU is a Chinese multitask benchmark with 67 subjects, including elementary_chinese, chinese_history and legal_and_moral_basis. When it came out, GPT-4 scored about 70% and most other models scored much lower. Recent frontier models and Chinese models such as Qwen and DeepSeek score above 85–90%.

guess: MATH (Hendrycks et al.), likely the MATH-500 subset, in a Llama 3.1 chat-template eval format
known_results: Llama 3.1 reports 0-shot CoT MATH scores of about 51.9% (8B), 68.0% (70B) and 73.8% (405B). Frontier reasoning models such as o1 and DeepSeek-R1 score above 90–96% on MATH-500.

DevBench (Tan et al., 2024) compares vision-language models such as CLIP, BLIP, and LLaVA with children's and adults' response patterns on lexical, syntactic (TROG), and semantic tasks. Models' answers resemble human answers to some degree. Models with better task accuracy tend to be more humanlike, but their patterns often look more like children's than adults'.

CRUXEval (Gu et al., 2024, Meta) contains 800 Python functions with input-prediction (CRUXEval-I) and output-prediction (CRUXEval-O) tasks. GPT-4 scored about 67% on input and 63% on output pass@1, and GPT-4 with CoT got roughly 75% and 81%. Later reasoning models (o1 and others) score above 90%.

EgoSchema is a long-form video QA benchmark built on 3-minute Ego4D clips. Early video-language models scored about 33% (close to random chance on 5 choices), while humans score about 76%. Later models like Gemini 1.5 Pro and GPT-4o reached roughly 70%+, and newer systems score in the high 70s.

EHRFlowBench was introduced with the HealthFlow self-evolving research-agent framework. It contains open-ended EHR analysis tasks built on TJH, MIMIC-IV-demo and similar datasets, and agent outputs are graded by LLM judges. HealthFlow was reported to beat general agents such as AI Scientist-style and Biomni/Alita-type baselines, but I don't recall exact scores, and the tasks remain challenging.

EditBench (Chi et al., 2025) is built from real instructed code edits collected through Copilot Arena, with highlighted code sections and instructions in many languages, and graded by tests. As I recall, about 40 models were evaluated and only a few passed more than 60% of tasks, with top models such as Claude Sonnet and GPT-4o-class systems around 60–65%.

guess: EngDesign (Toward Engineering AGI: Benchmarking the Engineering Design Capabilities of LLMs)
known_results: My recollection is that the top reasoning models, such as o3 and o4-mini, passed only about a third of the design tasks. Non-reasoning models scored lower, and many tasks went unsolved by every model. The tasks are checked by running simulations.

The ITFormer paper (ICML 2025) introduced this as a question-answering dataset built on aero-engine (C-MAPSS-style) time series, with understanding, perception, reasoning and decision-making tasks. As I recall, ITFormer clearly outperformed general-purpose LLMs and earlier time-series and language baselines, with accuracy and F1 scores on the multiple-choice tasks only moderate, roughly 60–80%. I'm not certain of the exact figures.

ERBench (Oh et al., 2024) checks both answer accuracy and whether the model's reasoning is correct. GPT-4 scored best but still hallucinated a lot, and models often gave the right answer with the wrong reasoning, especially on the negated and multi-hop questions.

guess: Natural Questions (open-domain, possibly mixed with TriviaQA)
known_results: Closed-book LLMs score roughly 30-50% exact match on NQ-Open. Retrieval-augmented systems reach around 50-60%. On TriviaQA, large models score above 80%.

BBH is 23 hard BIG-Bench tasks, including web_of_lies, causal_judgement and object_counting. The original paper found that chain-of-thought prompting let Codex and PaLM 540B beat average human raters on most tasks (about 73.9% for Codex with CoT). Frontier models now score around 90% or higher, so the benchmark is largely saturated.

In the original FinanceBench paper (Patronus AI, 2023), GPT-4-Turbo using a shared vector-store retrieval setup failed or refused on about 81% of the 150 sampled questions. Long-context and oracle-evidence setups did much better, and oracle setups reached roughly 70–85% accuracy.

In the original paper (CVPR 2024), GPT-4V scored best with about 31% question-pair accuracy and roughly 67% overall question accuracy. Most open-source vision-language models scored much lower, often near or below chance on the paired metrics, and showed strong language-prior hallucination and visual illusion failures.

Models usually score high on disambiguated contexts. On ambiguous contexts, weaker models often fall back on stereotypes when the correct answer is "unknown". Strong RLHF-trained models such as Claude and GPT-4 report high accuracy on ambiguous items and low bias scores, often around 90% or more.

guess: African-language translations of MMLU (clinical/virology) and Winogrande (Winogrande-ZA / MMLU-Clinical-ZA, part of AfroBench)
known_results: As I recall, models such as GPT-4o score far below their English results in low-resource languages like Bambara and Tsonga, sometimes close to chance on Winogrande. Fine-tuning on the translated data narrowed that gap somewhat.

When HLE came out in early 2025, frontier models scored very low on it, with GPT-4o at about 3% and o1 at about 9%. By late 2025, the best models with tools and reasoning reached roughly 25–45%, and calibration errors stayed high.

ThaiExam (from SCB10X, used in HELM Thai and the Thai LLM Leaderboard) covers ONET, IC, TGAT, TPAT-1 and A-Level exams. Frontier models such as GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet score roughly 60–80%, and open Thai models such as Typhoon and OpenThaiGPT score lower.

In the IgakuQA paper (Kasai et al., 2023), GPT-4 passed all five years of exams (2018–2022) with roughly 75–80% accuracy, while ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) failed. Later models such as GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 and o1 score about 85–95%, well above the passing threshold.

guess: IgakuQA (Japanese National Medical Licensing Examination benchmark), possibly a newer-year variant such as IgakuQA119
known_results: In the original IgakuQA paper (Kasai et al., 2023), GPT-4 passed the exam at roughly 78–82%, ChatGPT/GPT-3.5 did not pass, and the scores were below the average for students. Newer frontier models (o1, Claude, Gemini) are reported to score about 85–95% on recent exam years.

In the original KMMLU paper, GPT-4 scored about 59.95%, and the best open models were well below that, compared with a human pass threshold of about 80%. Later frontier models have reported scores of roughly 70–80% or more.

KorMedMCQA covers Korean licensing exams for doctors, nurses, pharmacists and dentists. Strong proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4o, o1) score around 75–90% overall, and the dentist subset is generally the hardest, with lower scores.

LegalBench (Guha et al., 2023) has 162 legal reasoning tasks, including function_of_decision_section and international_citizenship_questions. GPT-4 was the strongest model in the original paper, with an average of roughly 70–80% across task categories, and open models scored much lower. The citizenship questions were among the hardest tasks, with scores not far above chance.

LingOly (Bean et al., 2024, NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks) uses UK Linguistics Olympiad puzzles on low-resource languages. Models struggled with it: the top model, Claude 3 Opus, reached only about 46% exact match, and scores were much lower on the hardest problems. A follow-up benchmark, LingOly-TOO, adds obfuscated versions of the puzzles to reduce memorisation.

guess: Sports-Fitness (SportsFit) node classification dataset from CS-TAG / text-attributed graph benchmarks (e.g., GLBench, LLMNodeBed)
known_results: From what I remember, zero-shot LLMs that classify using only the product title get roughly 60–80% accuracy. Supervised GNNs and graph-LLM methods that use the co-purchase graph structure tend to score about 90% or higher.

true_names: LLMs-Lean historical evaluations of miniF2F and miniCTX | llms_lean_formalization
known_results: miniF2F has 488 olympiad-style problems (from MATH, AMC, AIME and IMO), split into valid and test sets. On the test set, pass rates went from about 30–40% for early systems (GPT-f, HTPS) to 60–70% for DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 and InternLM-Prover. By 2025, Kimina-Prover, DeepSeek-Prover-V2 and Seed-Prover were reporting 80–99%.

The "Hint: Please answer the question and provide the correct option letter" format comes from MathVista (testmini, 1000 items, including geometry from Geometry3K/GeoQA). GPT-4V scored about 49.9% and humans about 60.3%. Later models score higher: Gemini, Claude and GPT-4o reach roughly 60–70%, and reasoning models go past 80%.

guess: EHRSQL (eICU subset, as used in Stanford's MedHELM)
known_results: EHRSQL is a text-to-SQL benchmark built on the MIMIC-III and eICU databases, and it includes questions that cannot be answered from the data. In MedHELM, frontier LLMs score fairly low on it (execution accuracy roughly in the 20–40% range), making it one of the harder tasks in that suite.

HEAD-QA uses questions from the Spanish healthcare specialization exams (MIR, psychology and others), with English translations. Early IR and neural baselines scored only about 30–45%, while modern large LLMs score roughly 80–90% or higher on the English multiple-choice version.
GPT-4 scored about 86% and Med-PaLM 2 about 86.5%. Frontier models such as o1 and GPT-5 now score above 90–95%, while early models like PubMedBERT scored around 38–45%.

MedMCQA is a set of 4-option questions taken from Indian medical entrance exams (AIIMS/NEET PG), covering subjects such as dentistry and pharmacology. In the original paper, baseline models like PubMedBERT scored about 40-47%. Later, Med-PaLM 2 reached about 72%, and GPT-4-class models reach the high 70s to over 80%.

Medbullets comes from Chen et al. (2024), and it has USMLE Step 2/3-style questions with 4 or 5 answer options. It is harder than MedQA: in that paper GPT-4 scored about 64–68% on the 5-option version and much lower on the 4-option version. Newer frontier models score around 80% or higher.

Even top models like GPT-4o reach only about 0.625 F1 on the hard subset of detecting medical hallucinations. General-purpose LLMs often beat medical fine-tuned ones, and adding a 'not sure' option improves precision and F1.

On PubMedQA (reasoning-required setting), humans score about 78% accuracy. Fine-tuned BioBERT reached about 68%. Recent large models score in the high 70s to low 80s: Med-PaLM 2 got about 81.8%, and GPT-4 got roughly 75–82%.

guess: RaceBias (MedHELM; based on Omiye et al. 2023, "Large language models propagate race-based medicine")
known_results: Omiye et al. found that ChatGPT, GPT-4, Bard and Claude sometimes repeated debunked race-based medical claims, such as race-adjusted eGFR and lung capacity. In MedHELM, the classification version was relatively easy, and frontier models scored high accuracy at spotting race-based or inaccurate answers.

MJ-Bench tests multimodal judges (CLIP-based scorers, open-source VLMs, closed VLMs) on preference pairs covering alignment, safety, quality/artifacts and bias. Closed models like GPT-4o and Gemini Ultra were the best judges overall, while smaller scoring models did fairly well on alignment and quality. Open VLMs did worse, and their results depended a lot on whether the rating scale was numeric or narrative.

MMBench (OpenCompass) tests about 20 ability dimensions, including image style, function reasoning and nature relation, using multiple-choice questions scored with CircularEval. Early models like MiniGPT-4 scored around 20–40%, GPT-4V scored about 75–77%, and recent models such as InternVL, Qwen2-VL and GPT-4o score above 80–88%.
MMLU-Pro (TIGER-Lab, 2024) has up to 10 options per question across 14 subjects. GPT-4o scored about 72.6% at release. Later frontier models score around 80–90%.

The 5-shot MMLU from Hendrycks et al. (2020) has 57 subjects. GPT-3 scored about 44%, GPT-4 about 86%, and current frontier models reach roughly 88–92%, close to the ceiling set by label noise. Human expert-level performance is estimated at about 89.8%.

true_names: Large Language Monkeys: Monkey Business | monkey_power_laws
known_results: Minerva 540B scored about 50% (majority voting raised it further) and GPT-4 about 42% at release. Recent reasoning models score above 90%, so the benchmark is largely saturated.
SWE-bench Verified is a set of 500 human-validated GitHub issues, many of them from Django. Top agentic systems went from about 50% in late 2024 to over 70–80% resolved by 2025.

guess: LongGenBench (Wu et al., 2024 – long-form generation benchmark with skyscraper/urban planning/diary/menu tasks)
known_results: Long-context LLMs did poorly at following the specific, range and periodic instructions over very long outputs (16K–32K tokens), and their accuracy dropped as the output got longer. In the paper's results, larger models such as GPT-4o, Qwen2-72B and Gemini-1.5 did best, but even these were far from perfect.

guess: MTBBench (Molecular Tumor Board benchmark, using the HANCOCK cohort)
known_results: As I recall, this is an agentic benchmark that tests multimodal clinical reasoning over time. Frontier vision-language models scored only modestly, often not much above chance on outcome and recurrence questions, and gave tools and other agent setups improved results.

guess: NAEP (National Assessment of Educational Progress) released items, from the NAEP Questions Tool
known_results: The items come from the NAEP Questions Tool on nationsreportcard.gov and cover reading and math. I don't reliably remember published AI scores for an NAEP-based benchmark. Modern LLMs probably score well above average U.S. students on most multiple-choice items.

guess: Indirect Object Identification (IOI) dataset (Wang et al., 2022; also used in the Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark, MIB)
known_results: GPT-2 small picks the correct indirect object over the repeated subject most of the time, with a logit difference of about 3+. Larger models get near-perfect accuracy. The task is mainly used for circuit discovery (name mover heads, S-inhibition heads) rather than for comparing capabilities.

LLM agents solve only a small fraction of the 200 CSAW challenges: the original paper reported GPT-4-based agents at a few percent, and later agents such as EnIGMA reached around 13%, with other frameworks at roughly 10–20%.

PKU-Alignment's safety preference datasets pair harmful prompts with responses labeled for helpfulness and harmlessness. They're mainly used to train and evaluate safe RLHF (e.g., Beaver models). Safety-tuned models usually reach high harmlessness rates, while base models often comply with these prompts.

LLMs like GPT-4 scored very low on Mystery Blocksworld plan generation (often under 5%), even though they did much better on plain Blocksworld. Reasoning models like o1-preview did a lot better (around 50% or more on some splits), but they still fell short on the obfuscated domains and on longer plans.

This looks like PeruMedQA, a benchmark built from Peruvian medical residency (CONAREME) exam questions. I recall that large frontier models like GPT-4o and medgemma-27b scored well, above about 80%, and that small LLMs did worse but improved after fine-tuning. The Peruvian Spanish wording points to this benchmark, but HEAD-QA, which uses Spanish MIR exams, is also possible.

Early Isabelle provers like Thor and DSP got roughly 30–40% on the miniF2F test set. Later systems (LEGO-Prover, Lyra, SubgoalXL) raised this to about 45–56%, and the Lean-based provers that followed now score above 80–90%.

guess: REAL (Realistic Evaluations for Agents Leaderboard / REAL Bench by AGI, Inc.)
known_results: REAL runs web agents on deterministic copies of real websites, for example Omnizon (an Amazon clone), Staynb (an Airbnb clone) and Udriver (an Uber clone). As I recall, frontier models scored low when it came out, with the best near 40% overall success, though I'm not certain of the exact figure.

RealTime QA (Kasai et al., 2022) is a dynamic benchmark built from weekly news quizzes (CNN, The Week, USA Today). Models without retrieval do poorly on new questions because their knowledge is out of date. Retrieval-augmented GPT-3/GPT-4 setups do much better, reaching high multiple-choice accuracy, but their generation accuracy suffers when the retrieved documents are stale.

GPQA Diamond has 198 graduate-level multiple-choice questions written to be "Google-proof". Expert validators score about 65% and skilled non-experts about 34%. GPT-4 scored around 36–39% at release, while frontier reasoning models (o1, o3, Gemini 2.5, Claude 4 series, GPT-5) reach roughly 78–88% or more.
RISEBench tests reasoning-informed visual editing in temporal, causal, spatial and logical categories. GPT-4o-Image scored best, at only about 29% accuracy; open-source models scored close to zero.

guess: FLORES-200 (romanized Arabic/Arabizi variant of FLORES devtest sentences)
known_results: The source sentences are from FLORES (Wikinews/Wikivoyage/Wikibooks). The usual metrics are chrF++ and BLEU. LLMs score much worse on romanized or Arabizi input than on Arabic script.

SketchJudge tests whether multimodal LLMs can grade hand-drawn STEM diagrams (geometry, physics, charts, flowcharts) against a reference and label the error types. As I recall, even strong models like GPT-4o and Gemini scored well below human graders, especially at classifying errors.

StatQA (Zhu et al., NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks) tests whether LLMs can pick the right statistical methods and columns and judge when a method applies. Even the best models such as GPT-4o reached only about 64.8% accuracy with prompting. Fine-tuned smaller models such as LLaMA-3 did better, and human experts still beat the models at judging whether a method is applicable.
CLIP-style models do well on the add and replace splits (often 80-90%+) but worse on swap. Strong generative VLMs that are asked to pick between two captions score near ceiling on many subsets.

Earnings-call QA dataset (Pardawala et al., NeurIPS 2024 D&B) with six subjective features rated 0-2; fine-tuned RoBERTa/FinBERT roughly match or beat zero-shot LLMs, with weighted F1 mostly around 0.5-0.65. It is also included in the FLaME financial LLM evaluation suite.

τ²-bench is Sierra's follow-up to τ-bench. It covers retail, airline and telecom domains, and in the telecom domain the user also uses tools (dual control). In early tests, GPT-4.1-class models scored much lower on telecom (around 34%) than on retail. Later frontier models (Claude Opus 4.x, GPT-5) reached about 80% on retail and 80–98% on telecom.

In the original paper, GPT-4o function-calling agents scored about 35% pass^1 on the airline domain, and pass^k reliability fell sharply as k increased. Later frontier models such as Claude 3.7/4 Sonnet and GPT-4.1/o-series scored roughly 50–60% or higher on airline, and newer models pushed scores higher still.
Java issue-resolution tasks are hard for agents. Resolve rates for leading models with agent frameworks were reported at roughly 10–30% on the Java split, well below SWE-bench Verified Python scores.

In the original paper (Lin et al., 2021), the largest models were often the least truthful: GPT-3 175B scored about 21% on MC1, and humans scored about 94% on the generation task. Later instruction-tuned and RLHF models score much higher, with GPT-4 at about 60% MC1 after RLHF and frontier models above 80% on some variants.

In the Self-Instruct paper (Wang et al., 2022), expert humans rated model outputs on these items. GPT-3 tuned with Self-Instruct got close to InstructGPT-001: it was only about 5% behind. Vanilla GPT-3 did much worse. Later papers such as Alpaca also used the set for evaluation.

My recollection is that the 2025 TUMLU paper evaluated several large models. Top proprietary models such as Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro led with roughly 70–85% accuracy, while open models scored much lower, especially in languages with fewer resources (Crimean Tatar, Karakalpak) and when the questions were in Cyrillic or Arabic script.

Frontier models scored modestly when the benchmark was released. GPT-4o got about 65.8% overall accuracy and Gemini-1.5-Pro about 62.5%, while open-source VLMs often scored near chance (around 50%) on pairwise multimodal judgment, especially on the reasoning and hallucination subsets.

In the original MedCalc-Bench paper (Khandekar et al., 2024), GPT-4 with one-shot chain-of-thought prompting scored the highest, at about 50% accuracy. Open models scored much lower, and later reasoning and tool-using models have reported scores above 70–80%.

The original WorkArena atomic tasks were fairly solvable: GPT-4 scored about 40–55%. WorkArena++ compositional tasks were much harder, with GPT-4o and similar models solving only a small fraction (low single digits to about 15%) while humans scored about 94%.

In the original paper, the best agent was GPT-4 with ReAct, which completed about 43% of tasks. Weaker models such as Llama2-70B scored in the low single digits. Agents also often made unintended, harmful changes to the database.

guess: SemEval-2013 Task 7: Joint Student Response Analysis (SciEntsBank / Beetle)
known_results: The original systems scored roughly 0.5–0.7 macro/weighted F1 on the 5-way task, and did worse on the unseen-domain split. Later fine-tuned BERT-style models reached about 0.75–0.8+ on the 3-way and 2-way splits.

guess: SWE-rebench (Nebius SWE-bench-extra style dataset of GitHub issues)
known_results: It's a SWE-bench-style task set: real GitHub issues from many Python repos, such as darker, zope.schema and dvc, that the model must resolve with a patch that passes the tests. On SWE-rebench leaderboards, frontier agentic models usually resolve about 30–60% of tasks, and older or open models score much lower.

In the original AppWorld paper (Trivedi et al., ACL 2024), GPT-4o with ReAct reached about 49% task goal completion on Test-Normal and about 30% on Test-Challenge, and scenario goal completion was lower. Later agents have scored considerably higher.

KernelBench (Stanford, 2025) asks models to write CUDA kernels that are both correct and faster than the PyTorch reference, across Levels 1 to 3 (single ops, fused operators, full architectures). Frontier models originally beat the PyTorch baseline on only a small share of tasks (fast_1 often under 20% at one shot). Results improved substantially with iterative refinement and RL-trained agents.

BABILong hides bAbI QA tasks (qa1–qa20) inside long distractor text taken from PG19, at lengths up to millions of tokens. Most LLMs use only about 10–20% of their context well, and accuracy falls sharply as length grows. Fine-tuned recurrent memory transformers and retrieval-augmented models do much better on very long inputs than GPT-4 and other long-context LLMs.

guess: MEDEC (Medical Error Detection and Correction, MEDIQA-CORR 2024 shared task)
known_results: In the MEDEC paper (Ben Abacha et al., 2024), LLMs such as GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, o1-preview and Gemini were tested on detecting and correcting errors. The best models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet for error flagging, o1-preview for correction) did reasonably well, with roughly 60-70% accuracy at detecting errors, but they still did worse than physicians, especially at finding the exact error sentence and correcting it.

AlgoTune (2025) has about 155 numerical and algorithmic tasks. Language-model agents try to write code that runs faster than reference solutions built on SciPy, NumPy and CVXPY. Frontier models got average speedups of roughly 1.7–2x, mostly from surface-level optimizations rather than new algorithms.

guess: WorldsCentralBanks (WCB) – Words That Unite the World central bank communication benchmark
known_results: The benchmark covers about 25 central banks and three tasks: stance, temporal (forward-looking) and certainty. As I recall, fine-tuned models trained on data from all the banks outperformed zero-shot and few-shot LLMs, which only reached moderate F1 scores, and the uncertainty and temporal tasks were hard for them.

true_names: MasakhaNER 1.0 and 2.0: released NER predictions | afrieval
guess: MasakhaNER (Twi test set, original MasakhaNER 1.0 BIO tagging)
known_results: MasakhaNER is a named entity recognition dataset for African languages (Adelani et al., 2021), with PER, ORG, LOC and DATE tags. Fine-tuned models such as AfroXLMR and mT5 reach about 80–90 F1 on many languages. Twi is one of the harder ones, with F1 in the 60s–70s. Zero-shot LLM prompting generally scores lower than fine-tuned models.

guess: Exercism-based coding benchmark (e.g., Aider Polyglot, which uses Exercism exercises in C++ and other languages)
known_results: The items are Exercism exercises (spiral-matrix, classification of numbers, binary search tree) with C++ starter files. This matches the Aider Polyglot benchmark, which has 225 hard Exercism problems across 6 languages. Frontier models score roughly 60-90% on it, depending on the model and the edit format used. I'm not certain it is Polyglot and not a similar Exercism-derived set.

guess: BIRD (BIg Bench for LaRge-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL Evaluation)
known_results: The BIRD dev set has databases such as superhero, california_schools and codebase_community. Execution accuracy is the main metric. Human performance is about 92.96%. Early GPT-4 results were about 54%, and later specialized systems reach roughly 70-75% on the dev or test set.

BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022) tests social bias with ambiguous and disambiguated contexts. Models usually score high on disambiguated items. They score lower on ambiguous items, where they tend to follow stereotypes instead of choosing "unknown". These items are all disambiguated, so strong modern models get them almost all correct (above 90%).

guess: BIRD (BIg Bench for LaRge-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL Evaluation), dev set
known_results: The BIRD dev set has 1,534 questions. Execution accuracy was about 50-60% for early LLM baselines such as ChatGPT. Top systems with GPT-4 or o1-class models and agentic pipelines reach about 70-76% on dev. Human performance is about 92.96%.

Belebele is Meta's multilingual reading comprehension benchmark covering 122 language variants. Large LLMs score high on English, but low-resource languages like Northern Sotho score much lower. Top models such as GPT-4 reach roughly 50–80% on these languages, and smaller models score near chance (25%). I don't recall exact figures for this language.

HallusionBench tests image-context reasoning with yes/no questions, split into Visual Dependent (VD) and Visual Supplement (VS) categories. GPT-4V scored about 65% question-level accuracy and about 31% on paired-question accuracy at release. Open-source models scored lower, and even later frontier models stayed well below human performance.

In PlanBench (Valmeekam et al.), the obfuscated Mystery Blocksworld was very hard for LLMs: GPT-4 solved only a few percent. Reasoning models like o1 do much better but still fail on many instances, especially the longer ones.

I'm not certain these three items come from it, since the prompts could also come from a related instruction dataset.

WorkArena++ is a ServiceNow benchmark of compositional, long-horizon enterprise workflow tasks, including change request scheduling and list sorting. Agents score low. GPT-4o-based agents solve only a few percent of tasks, and humans score much higher. I don't remember exact figures.

WorkBench (Styles et al., 2024) is a workplace-simulation benchmark with five databases (email, calendar, web analytics, CRM, project management) and 26 tools. I recall GPT-4 scoring about 43% and weaker open models such as Llama2-70B scoring very low, around 3%. Many failures came from wrong or unintended side-effect actions.

guess: SWE-bench Multimodal / multi-language GitHub issue resolution (SWE-Gym or SWE-bench-extra style, e.g., nemotron/SWE-rebench)
known_results: Not sure of the exact benchmark. The items look like GitHub issues from Python repos (darker, zope.schema, dvc), which fits SWE-Gym or SWE-rebench style datasets. Top agents resolve roughly 50-70% on SWE-bench Verified, and I can't give a specific score for this one.

AppWorld tasks use simulated apps (Amazon, Spotify, SimpleNote, Gmail) with API-based agents. Frontier LLM agents scored low at launch (GPT-4o about 49% on test-normal, about 30% on test-challenge). Newer agents have scored much higher.

guess: MEDEC (MEDEC: A Benchmark for Medical Error Detection and Correction in Clinical Notes)
known_results: MEDEC (Microsoft/UW, 2024) has clinical notes from MedQA-derived and MS/UW sources, with error detection, sentence ID extraction and correction tasks. LLMs like GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and o1-preview score well below physicians on error detection and correction. Claude 3.5 Sonnet did relatively well at detection and o1-preview was best overall.

KernelBench (Stanford, Ouyang et al. 2025) tasks LLMs with writing fast CUDA kernels to replace PyTorch Model modules. Frontier models produce correct and faster kernels (fast_1) on only a minority of tasks, especially at Level 1. Reasoning models like o1 and DeepSeek-R1 did best, and results improve with iterative refinement and execution feedback.

BABILong embeds bAbI task facts (qa1–qa20) in long PG19 distractor text. LLMs do well at short contexts, but accuracy falls sharply as length grows. Models often use only 10–20% of their stated context window effectively. RAG and fine-tuned recurrent-memory models do better on some tasks.

AlgoTune (2025) asks LMs to write code that runs faster than reference solvers (scipy, cvxpy, etc.) across about 150 tasks. It scores by average speedup over the reference, and the best models, such as o4-mini and DeepSeek R1, reached only about 1.5–2x average speedup. I'm not certain of the exact figures.

true_names: MasakhaNER 1.0 and 2.0: released NER predictions | afrieval
known_results: MasakhaNER (Adelani et al., 2021) is a named-entity recognition dataset of news text in African languages, including Twi, with PER/ORG/LOC/DATE tags in BIO format. Fine-tuned multilingual and African-language pretrained encoders (e.g., AfroXLMR) score roughly in the 70s to 80s F1 on Twi, and it was later extended as MasakhaNER 2.0.

KOR-Bench (Knowledge-Orthogonal Reasoning) tests rule induction over redefined operators and symbols, such as base-4 arithmetic, custom functions, and ciphers, so models must reason rather than recall. From memory, frontier models score well below human level on its harder categories, though I am not certain of exact figures.

BIRD is a large text-to-SQL benchmark with messy real-world databases, external-knowledge evidence hints, and execution-accuracy scoring; the items match its format (db_id, evidence field, schemas like superhero, california_schools, codebase_community). Systems scored roughly 40-55% at launch in 2023 versus about 92% for human experts, and frontier LLM systems have since climbed well above 60-70% on the dev set.

The items are Exercism exercises (spiral matrix, perfect numbers, binary search tree) in C++ with initial files, which matches Aider's polyglot benchmark of about 225 hard Exercism problems across C++, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python and Rust. Models are scored by the share of problems whose solutions pass the hidden tests, and frontier models have reported scores in roughly the 60-90%+ range, though I am not certain of exact figures.

BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022) tests social biases across nine categories using ambiguous and disambiguated context-question pairs with "unknown"-style options. Models typically score high on disambiguated items but often fall back on stereotyped answers when the context is ambiguous, so bias scores are the key result.

BIRD is a large-scale text-to-SQL benchmark with dirty database values and external "evidence" hints, scored by execution accuracy; the items match its format (database_id such as toxicology, student_club, codebase_community). At its release, the best systems scored roughly 40-55% on the dev set versus about 92% for human experts, and later LLM-based agent systems have reached the high 60s to 70s percent.

guess: WMDP (Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy), biology subset
known_results: WMDP-Bio is a multiple-choice set of hazardous-knowledge biology questions, and its prompts appear to follow an MMLU-style template. Frontier models typically score well above chance (around 60–80%), and it is used to measure whether unlearning methods reduce hazardous knowledge.

The '#C C' (camera wearer) and '#O' (other person) narration tags, and the 180-second clip length, match the Charades-Ego egocentric/third-person video dataset, which is typically used for action recognition and video-language tasks. I don't reliably recall specific AI model scores on it, so treat this identification as tentative.

BIG-Bench Hard is a 23-task subset of BIG-Bench (Suzgun et al., 2022) where early language models performed below the average human rater; these items match its Web of Lies, Causal Judgment, and Object Counting tasks. Chain-of-thought prompting substantially improved scores, and recent frontier models score very high, with many reported near or above 90% average accuracy.

BBQ, from Parrish et al. (2022), tests social biases across nine categories using ambiguous and disambiguated contexts with "unknown"/"cannot be determined" options. Models answer disambiguated items fairly accurately but often fall back on stereotypes in ambiguous contexts, so bias scores are the main reported metric.

The items are Thai-language multiple-choice questions drawn from Thai exams (investment consultant licensing, ONET-style science, math, and Thai-language reading), which fits my recollection of ThaiExam, a Thai exam benchmark. I don't reliably recall specific per-model scores, but multilingual and Thai-focused models generally score well above random on it, with the investment-license and professional-exam sections being harder.
Frontier models scored low at launch in early 2025, under about 10% on the text-and-image set. Scores have risen substantially since, though I am not certain of current figures.

The items look like Korean national licensing and certification exam questions (calculus, physics, biochemical engineering), which matches KMMLU, a Korean multiple-choice benchmark built from such exams. I recall frontier models scoring well above the 25% chance baseline but well below expert-human level, though I don't remember exact figures.

LingOly is a benchmark of linguistics olympiad-style puzzles (drawn from International and UK olympiad problems) on low-resource languages and writing systems. Frontier models have scored well below human olympiad competitors, with reported accuracies roughly in the 30–50% range on the hardest subsets.

true_names: LLMs-Lean historical evaluations of miniF2F and miniCTX | llms_lean_formalization
known_results: miniF2F is a benchmark of olympiad and competition math problems (AMC, AIME, IMO, MATH-derived) formalized in Lean, Isabelle, and Metamath, with the Lean version widely used for neural theorem proving. Recent LLM-based provers have reached roughly 50-60%+ on the miniF2F test split, while early models scored much lower.

EHRSQL (Lee et al., 2022, ML4H) is a text-to-SQL benchmark over MIMIC-III/IV and eICU EHR schemas, and its prompts include unanswerable questions that should return an empty string. I recall that fine-tuned T5-style models and few-shot LLMs were reported with substantially lower scores than on standard text-to-SQL benchmarks, but I don't reliably recall the exact figures.
These are USMLE-style four-option clinical vignettes, consistent with MedQA. Early LLMs scored roughly 50-60% on the four-option set, and recent frontier models report scores above 90%.

PubMedQA is a yes/no/maybe biomedical question-answering benchmark built from PubMed abstracts, with 1,000 expert-labeled test questions. Reported results: human performance around 78%, fine-tuned BioBERT around 73%, and frontier LLMs in the high 70s to low 80s percent accuracy, often with reasoning or few-shot prompting.

known_results: The items match the race-based medicine prompts from Omiye et al. (npj Digital Medicine, 2023), covering eGFR race coefficients, spirometry race correction, and skin thickness by race. In that study, several then-current chatbots, including GPT-4, often reproduced debunked race-based clinical claims rather than rejecting them.

Multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects (here college CS, high school geography, professional law), introduced by Hendrycks et al. (2020) with a 5-shot format. Random guessing scores about 25%; GPT-4 scored about 86% and recent frontier models score roughly 88-92%, near the estimated human expert level of about 89%.

known_results: The items are few-shot exemplars in the Minerva-style "Final Answer: The final answer is ... I hope it is correct." format used for competition-math problems from the MATH dataset. Early models scored low (Minerva 540B about 50% with few-shot prompting in 2022), and frontier models now score above 90%, so the benchmark is largely saturated.

The ten-option multiple-choice format across economics, business arithmetic, and biology matches MMLU-Pro, an expanded and harder successor to MMLU. Frontier models typically score roughly in the 70s to 80s percent on it, with the exact figures depending on the model and evaluation setup.

HANCOCK is a multimodal head-and-neck squamous cell carcinoma dataset that pairs H&E whole-slide images, immune-cell IHC staining (CD3, CD8, CD56, CD68, CD163), and clinical records. I don't recall published AI scores on it, so I can't say how systems perform.

I do not recall published AI model scores on this specific set.

miniF2F is a cross-system benchmark of 488 formalized competition problems (AMC, AIME, IMO, and MATH-style) in Lean, Isabelle, and Metamath, split into validation and test sets. Scores on it have risen steadily, with LLM-based provers reaching roughly 90%+ on the Lean version, while Isabelle results are generally lower and less reported.

These items look like the obfuscated 'Mystery Blocksworld' domain from PlanBench (Valmeekam et al., 2023), where the blocksworld actions and predicates are renamed (e.g., pick-up, stack, and holding become Attack, Overcome, and Pain). Early LLMs scored very poorly on the obfuscated version, in the single-digit percent range, while later reasoning models improved substantially but remained well below their scores on standard blocksworld.

Items are simulated customer-service tasks with domain policies (retail, telecom) and tool calls, matching the τ-bench / τ²-bench family from Sierra. Models are scored by pass^k reliability on the tasks, and telecom is generally reported as the hardest domain, with many models scoring well below retail.

TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2021) has 817 questions designed to elicit common human misconceptions, and the items here use its few-shot 'I have no comment' format with misconception-prone questions. When it was introduced, the largest models were often less truthful than smaller ones because they imitated popular false beliefs, with GPT-3 around 58% truthful versus about 94% for humans.

These are simulated-user instructions from the airline domain of τ-bench (Sierra), where an LLM user simulator tests an agent on flight changes and cancellations under policy rules, such as basic-economy restrictions and refund eligibility. In the original paper, frontier models scored well below human-level reliability on airline tasks, with pass^k consistency dropping sharply as k increases.

MedCalc-Bench (Stanford, 2024) tests LLMs on computing clinical values such as formulas like Hodges QTc from patient notes, with about 1,000 test cases across many calculators. Reported accuracy was modest for early models (roughly 30-50% in one-shot settings), with newer frontier models scoring substantially higher, though exact figures vary by setting.

These are ServiceNow browser tasks (list filtering, sorting, and change-request scheduling), which fits WorkArena or its harder follow-up WorkArena++. As I recall, frontier models do well on the simpler single-step tasks but score much lower on the multi-step compositional ones.

KernelBench (Stanford, 2025) tests whether LLMs can write faster GPU kernels than PyTorch reference implementations across three levels: single operators, fused operator sequences, and full architectures. Models are scored on whether generated kernels are correct and on a fast_p metric (correct and faster than the baseline), and most frontier models have scored low on the harder levels.

BABILONG hides bAbI-style facts (single and multi-fact location, object-tracking, and spatial reasoning questions) inside long distractor text, such as PG19 books, to test long-context reasoning. Reported results show strong models scoring well on short contexts but degrading sharply as context length grows, with retrieval-augmented methods generally weaker than full-context inference.

true_names: MasakhaNER 1.0 and 2.0: released NER predictions | afrieval
known_results: MasakhaNER (Adelani et al., 2021) is a named-entity recognition benchmark for African languages (Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, Swahili, Twi, Wolof, Amharic, Xhosa, Zulu, Somali) with BIO tags. It reports F1 scores for models like XLM-R and AfriBERTa; large multilingual models typically score roughly 60-75% F1 depending on language, with performance on lower-resource languages like Twi and Wolof generally weaker than on Hausa or Swahili.

BIRD is a large-scale cross-domain text-to-SQL benchmark (HKU, ~12,751 questions over 95 databases) where models translate natural-language questions into SQL, with an 'evidence'/hint field as shown. Published leaderboards show strong models scoring in the ~50-60% execution-accuracy range (GPT-4 ~54%, and recent fine-tuned/agentic systems reaching ~60-75%), well below the ~90%+ human baseline.

MMLU is a 57-subject multiple-choice benchmark spanning STEM, humanities, social sciences, and professional knowledge (e.g., marketing, elementary math, medicine), which matches this mix of items. Historically, GPT-4 scored around 86% (5-shot), strong chat models reach 80-90%, and the reported human-expert baseline is about 89.8%.

BBQ tests whether QA models rely on social biases in ambiguous contexts; large language models, especially after instruction tuning, often score well by choosing the 'Unknown/Undetermined' option, but many earlier models showed systematic bias, and models often display bias when contexts are disambiguated in the biased direction.

BasqueEval is a multiple-choice trivia QA benchmark developed by the Basque NLP community (HiTZ Center / IXA, University of the Basque Country), with questions in Basque and Spanish covering general knowledge. It is a few-shot format (system prompt demanding a single A/B/C answer), and published results show large general-purpose LLMs scoring well above the random baseline, with performance generally lower on the Basque-language items than on Spanish.

guess: BIRD-SQL (BIRD: A Big Bench for Large Language Models Crossing Database and Reasoning)
known_results: BIRD is a large-scale text-to-SQL benchmark with cross-domain databases, where prompts include an 'evidence' hint field and the database schema; models must generate SQL for natural language questions. Published results show it is much harder than Spider: GPT-4-era systems score roughly 50-60% execution accuracy, best models around 70-75%, well below the ~90%+ human ceiling.

These are exercises from the Exercism coding platform (spiral matrix, perfect numbers, binary search tree), which have been packaged with instructions and starter files into a code-generation benchmark; a notable use is the paper 'Can Large Language Models Write Good Code?', which evaluated LLMs on Exercism exercises across languages. Frontier models generally score quite high on these tasks (roughly 80-90%+ pass rates), with results varying by programming language track, though I am not confident in the exact published numbers.

Belebele is Meta AI's multiple-choice reading comprehension benchmark covering 115 languages (including low-resource ones like Northern Sotho/Sepedi). Frontier LLMs tend to score well on high-resource languages but noticeably lower on low-resource African languages; smaller models score poorly across the board.

RealTimeQA (Kasai et al.) weekly asks models questions about very recent news events with short answers; models score far below humans, and closed-book models often default to guessing (hence the 'provide your most reasonable guess' instruction). The RAG-with-context variants shown here are reminiscent of its retrieval-augmented settings, but I am only moderately confident these specific prompt templates come from that benchmark rather than a similar news-QA evaluation.

These are competition-math word problems from the MATH dataset of Hendrycks et al. (2021), which asks models to produce final answers matched against exact reference answers. Frontier LLMs now score very high (often 70–90%+ with chain-of-thought or tool use), while older/smaller models historically scored much lower; the specific formatting here is a Llama-3 chat template, suggesting a harness-style evaluation run.

These match CRUXEval's two tasks: input prediction (given f(??) == output, produce an input) and output prediction (complete the assertion with the execution output). On the original CRUXEval (375 Python functions, input and output prediction with pass@1), GPT-4 scored around 70-75%, GPT-3.5 and open models like Llama and Mistral scored roughly 30-50%, and strong reasoning models later approached or exceeded 90%.

CMMLU is a Chinese multiple-choice exam benchmark covering dozens of subjects (from elementary/primary topics to law and history), with a prompt template requiring the final line in the format '答案: $选项'. Published results show GPT-4 and strong Chinese models (e.g., Qwen, ChatGLM) scoring in the roughly 55-70% range at release, with ChatGPT around 50%, and newer frontier models scoring much higher (85%+).

MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021) is a 57-subject multiple-choice benchmark; these items use its standard 'The following are multiple choice questions (with answers) about biology' prompt format. Typical scoring: random baseline ~25%, GPT-3 ~44%, modern frontier models score roughly 85-90%.

These items look like CyberGym tasks: each gives a real-world vulnerability (largely drawn from OSS-Fuzz/ARVO-style bugs such as Linux kernel Bluetooth L2CAP, libsepol, OpenSC) and asks the agent to analyze source code and produce a proof-of-concept that crashes the target binary, verified via a run.sh harness. Published results show frontier LLM agents achieve only modest success rates, with performance well below human/expert baselines on the harder levels of the benchmark.

FinanceBench is a benchmark of finance questions over SEC filings/earnings materials (10-Ks, 10-Qs, earnings releases), released by Patronus AI in late 2023 with 150 open-source questions. Published results showed all major LLMs performed poorly — best models scored roughly 40-50% accuracy (e.g., GPT-4-Turbo around 45-50% depending on setup), with retrieval-augmented setups still far below reliable accuracy, demonstrating that open-source models and even frontier LLMs struggle on financial QA.

The #C/#O tagging scheme (camera wearer vs. other people), 180-second clip durations, and dense third-person-style narration captions are characteristic of the Ego4D dataset's Narration track from Meta/FB's egocentric video benchmark. Ego4D is best known for its challenge tasks (NLQ, VQ/VQ2D, PNR, moment queries), where state-of-the-art video-language models still score relatively modestly; narration data itself is often used for dense captioning and long-video summarization evaluations.

These items match BIG-bench task styles: a truth-teller/liar logic puzzle (knights-and-knaves style), the 'causal judgment' task about typical-person intuitions (Knobe-effect style intentional attribution), and an object-counting task. I recall BIG-bench generally being hard for pre-2022 models, with best models scoring well below human level on many tasks, but I don't recall specific published scores for these particular tasks with high confidence.

guess: Jeopardy! (Jeopardy-derived QA benchmark, e.g., the J! Archive dataset used in HELM/SearchQA)
known_results: These are Jeopardy!-style trivia clues converted to questions. Jeopardy! datasets drawn from J! Archive have been used in evaluations like HELM, where large language models generally perform strongly on such factual recall questions, with accuracy rising steeply with model scale.

These read like text-to-image generation prompts from Google's Parti benchmark (or its companion DrawBench), which evaluate image generation with categories including text rendering and unusual/creative scenes. Parti reached strong human-evaluated photorealism with its Imagen/Parti models, though exact per-item scores are not something I can reliably recall; my confidence in this attribution is only moderate.

BBQ measures social bias in question answering using ambiguous contexts where the correct answer is 'Unknown/Cannot be determined', plus disambiguated cases. Large language models often show bias by answering with stereotype-consistent choices on ambiguous items; bias scores have generally decreased with newer/larger models, and instructing models to answer 'Unknown' reduces but does not always eliminate biased answers.

These items match BenchMAX, a multi-task multilingual benchmark suite (Cohere Labs, ~2025) that includes translated MMLU-style multiple-choice questions and translated Winogrande-style coreference sentences in many languages, including very low-resource ones like Bambara and Tsonga. Published results showed frontier models (e.g., GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Command R+) score far below their English performance on the low-resource languages, with Bambara among the weakest.

JMedBench is a Japanese biomedical benchmark built from Japan's national licensing examinations (medicine, pharmacy, nursing, dentistry), which matches the style of these clinical vignette multiple-choice items. Published results showed that large general-purpose LLMs score well below human passing thresholds on it, and domain-specific biomedical models did not clearly outperform strong general LLMs in the Japanese setting.

These look like the multiple-choice questions from KMMLU (Korean Massive Multitask Language Understanding), a benchmark of Korean exam-style questions across ~45 subjects from professional/licensing and high-school exams. Frontier models historically scored relatively low (roughly 50-60%), well below human expert performance (~60-70%), which was the benchmark's headline finding.

HLE (Scale AI / CAIS, 2025) contains ~2,500 extremely difficult expert questions across many domains, often with images and tricky answer-formatting instructions. Frontier models score low: roughly 10-20% without tools, and about 20-30% with search/tools for the best models (e.g., o3/GPT-5-class around ~25%).

LegalBench (Guha et al., 2023) is a collaborative benchmark of ~162 legal reasoning tasks, including small datasets like the function-of-decision-section classifier shown here (labeling paragraphs of judicial opinions as Facts, Issue, Rule, etc.) and international citizenship-law questions. It is also run as scenarios in Stanford HELM. Scores vary widely across its tasks; simple classification tasks like paragraph function labeling are near-saturated by modern LLMs, while harder reasoning tasks show much lower accuracy, and the benchmark reports both zero-shot and few-shot results for many open and commercial models.

MathVista is a multimodal math reasoning benchmark where models answer visual math questions, many with multiple-choice geometry problems like these. State-of-the-art VLMs and GPT-4V-class models score roughly 50–70% depending on version, well below human performance (~90%).

Strong LLMs score fairly high on it, but it has been shown to be considerably easier than harder biomedical benchmarks like PubMedQA or MedQA, with near-saturated scores for frontier models.

Models typically score well below expert human level on it; typical LLM accuracy is in the ~50-70% range depending on model scale, with top models in the 70s.

Reported accuracies there ranged from near-random for small models to roughly 50-90% for larger LLMs, with the answerable/unanswerable split being a key failure mode.

LLMs generally score very high on it; frontier models reach ~75-90%+ accuracy on the labeled subset, with GPT-4-class models around 80-90%, well above earlier fine-tuned models like BioBERT (~55%).

MMLU is a 57-subject multiple-choice benchmark (from Hendrycks et al., 2021) with the distinctive prompt format 'The following are multiple choice questions (with answers) about <subject>'. Frontier models typically score in the high-80s to around 90 percent accuracy, while early GPT-3-class models scored far lower and random guessing is ~25%.

MMLU-Pro is a harder version of MMLU with 10 answer choices per question (instead of 4) and more reasoning-focused items, which drops model scores substantially. Strong models at its release (2024) scored around 60-75% (e.g., GPT-4 around 72%), with newer reasoning models reaching roughly 80-90%.

Published results show LLMs like GPT-4 score near 0% on solvable instances in this obfuscated domain, while classical PDDL planners solve essentially all of them, demonstrating that LLM planning success in standard Blocksworld relies partly on memorization.

It is widely used to evaluate function-calling and task-oriented dialogue models via intent detection accuracy and slot F1; strong LLM-based systems now score very high on these classic metrics, while it also serves as a basis for function-calling evaluations.

These are user persona instructions from the airline domain of τ-bench (Sierra), which evaluates agents on tool use plus policy adherence and user-interaction skills in simulated customer service settings. Published results show even top models score relatively low (typically ~30-60% pass^1, much lower pass^k), with frontier models like GPT-4o, Claude, and o1 leading but far from saturating; retail domain scores are generally higher than airline.

The judge scores on it are typically weak, with even strong models showing only modest agreement with human preferences on these multimodal comparisons.

MedCalc-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on medical calculations (formulas like corrected QT, scores, etc.) drawn from clinical notes. At publication (2024), leading models scored relatively poorly—GPT-4-based systems achieved roughly 35–55% accuracy depending on category—well below expert clinicians.

These look like the compositional/planning ServiceNow tasks (e.g., scheduling change requests with risk-based durations, multi-field list sorting) from WorkArena++, which extends WorkArena with memory, reasoning, and planning task categories. Published results showed web agents built on LLMs score very low on these compositional tasks (often single-digit to ~20% success, depending on the model), while humans solve them almost perfectly.

These look like SWE-bench task instances (real GitHub issues from Python repos, e.g., here plone and dvc), where models must produce a repository patch that passes the repo's tests. On SWE-bench Verified, pass@1 has risen from ~2-4% for early models to roughly 30-50% for strong agents (e.g., GPT-4o-based agents ~30-40%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet-based agents ~50%) and higher for frontier models in 2025; SWE-bench Full/Lite are harder/filtered variants.

KernelBench (from Stanford, ~2025) is a benchmark of PyTorch workload definitions (nn.Module classes with get_inputs/get_init_inputs, organized into difficulty levels 1-4) used to test whether LLMs can write GPU kernels that are both correct and faster than PyTorch's eager/compiled baselines. Published results showed frontier models (e.g., Claude, GPT-4 class models) struggled: only a small fraction of generated kernels were functionally correct, and even fewer achieved meaningful speedups over baseline.

These tasks match AppWorld's style of multi-app agent tasks across simulated apps like SimpleNote, Amazon, Spotify, and Gmail. From what I recall, the benchmark is generally hard for LLM agents: frontier models with iterative coding agents score on the order of ~10-30% on the normal task set (with 'pass^k' metrics even lower), while simpler baseline agents score near zero.

These are bAbI-style tasks (Weston et al., 2015): object tracking/Where-was-object-before (qa6/qa1) and positional reasoning, wrapped in a few-shot prompt format. I recognize the task content, source (Facebook AI Research's bAbI suite, published with results showing early models failed on many of the 20 tasks), and typical modern results (large LLMs score near ceiling on short bAbI contexts but degrade as context grows, as shown in BABILong). CodeEditorBench evaluates code-editing abilities across tasks like bug fixing, translation, polishing, and requirement switching. It uses execution/correctness-based metrics such as pass@1; top proprietary and code-specialized models generally perform best, while smaller/open models lag.

CyberGym is a cybersecurity benchmark built from real-world OSS-Fuzz vulnerabilities, where agents analyze source/binaries and produce PoCs that reproduce crashes. Published results show low success rates, with even strong LLM agents solving only a minority of tasks.

BBH is a set of 23 challenging BIG-Bench tasks, including web_of_lies, causal_judgement, and object_counting. Chain-of-thought prompting substantially improves model performance, but frontier models still do not uniformly solve it; scores vary by task and model.
