Cybench is a CTF-style cybersecurity benchmark built from real competition challenges, including CSAW tasks like these. I recall top language-model agents solve only a modest fraction of its tasks, roughly under 20% in agentic settings.

guess: NAEP (National Assessment of Educational Progress) released items
known_results: These are released NAEP Questions Tool items, often used as an AI benchmark across grades/subjects. Reported AI performance tends to lag human student proficiency, especially on reading items and multi-step math, with scores varying by grade level and prompt format.

ScienceAgentBench contains data-driven scientific discovery tasks where agents must write and execute code. Reported LLM agent success rates are low, with the best systems solving only around a third of tasks, well below human expert performance.

These prompts match PlanBench's natural-language planning tasks, including the obfuscated Mystery domain with actions like Attack, Succumb, Overcome, and Feast. LLMs generally score poorly on PlanBench planning generation, especially on Mystery and longer-horizon instances, with many models near zero on exact plan validity.

miniF2F is a formal theorem-proving benchmark of olympiad/undergraduate-style math problems in Isabelle, Lean, Coq, and Metamath. AI systems generally score low on it; early neural/LLM provers solved only a small fraction, with later systems improving but remaining well below full coverage.

guess: HELM (Holistic Evaluation of Language Models), specifically its multimodal/VHELM image-generation evaluation
known_results: HELM/VHELM is a public Stanford CRFM evaluation suite; its image-generation scenarios use prompt sets such as DrawBench/PartiPrompts and include LLM-judge templates for dimensions like alignment and artifacts. I do not recall specific published score numbers for these exact text-to-image judge items.

GPQA is a graduate-level multiple-choice benchmark in physics, chemistry, and biology, with a Diamond subset often reported. Expert humans score around 65% on GPQA Diamond, while GPT-4 scored around 39% and newer frontier models have reached roughly 60–80% depending on the model and setting.
FreshQA is a dated current-events QA benchmark; models tend to score much lower on fast-changing and false-premise questions, while retrieval/search augmentation substantially improves accuracy.

I recall StatQA evaluates LLMs on statistical question answering, including selecting relevant columns and applicable statistical methods. Models such as GPT-4 perform well below human experts and often struggle to select all applicable methods.

Mind2Web is a generalist web-agent benchmark with thousands of natural-language tasks across many real websites. Reported results show agents still struggle on end-to-end task success, with evaluation typically using element accuracy, step success, and task success metrics.
It is a multilingual issue-resolution benchmark that asks systems to generate patches for real GitHub issues; the Java subset is challenging, and top agents resolve only a minority of instances.

τ²-bench is a tool-agent-user conversational benchmark with retail, airline, and telecom domains. AI systems generally score low, and pass^k reliability drops sharply versus pass^1, especially in dual-control telecom tasks.

τ-bench evaluates LLM agents in tool-agent-user conversations, including airline and retail customer-service domains, using success rate and pass^k reliability metrics. Models generally struggle, especially on the airline domain and on consistent multi-trial pass^k performance.

TruthfulQA tests whether models give truthful answers to questions designed to elicit common misconceptions. Large models often score modestly on it (e.g., MC1 accuracy commonly in the 20–40% range), well below human performance.

I recall Super-NaturalInstructions as a large collection of NLP tasks with natural-language instructions and examples. AI systems are typically evaluated on held-out tasks using metrics such as ROUGE-L and exact match, and strong instruction-tuned models perform best but generally remain well below human performance.

SWE-bench evaluates resolving real GitHub issues by generating patches, and top systems still resolve only a fraction of tasks (e.g., around 49% on SWE-bench Verified for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, with lower scores on the full set).

SugarCrepe is a vision-language compositional reasoning benchmark built from COCO-style captions with hard negative captions (replace/swap/add). CLIP-family models typically score well below human ceiling, often in the 70s–80s depending on split and model.

BixBench is an agentic bioinformatics benchmark built from real computational-biology tasks with file inspection and structured EVAL_ANSWER outputs. Frontier LLM agents generally score low, with many tasks requiring multi-step data analysis and exact-answer formatting.
MedCalc-Bench evaluates LLMs on computing medical calculator values from patient notes, requiring exact numeric answers. Models generally struggle, with top systems around 50% accuracy.

WorkArena is a browser-based benchmark built on ServiceNow, with tasks involving modules like Change and Asset. AI agents generally score poorly on it, with low task success rates compared with humans, especially on multi-step compositional tasks.

The WikiHow dataset is built from wikiHow articles and is commonly used for abstractive summarization/instruction-style generation, typically evaluated with ROUGE. Models generally score well below human performance because the summaries are abstractive and varied.

OfficeBench is a multi-application office-automation agent benchmark spanning calendar, email, CRM, project management, and analytics tasks. Strong LLM agents generally score low on it, especially on multi-app tasks, with best models succeeding on only a fraction of tasks.

ASAP-SAS is a short-answer scoring benchmark built from science prompts with human-scored student responses. AI systems are typically evaluated by agreement with human scores, often using quadratic weighted kappa, with strong systems achieving high but not perfect agreement.

KernelBench evaluates whether LLMs can generate correct and fast GPU kernels (e.g., CUDA/Triton) implementing PyTorch model operations, scored on correctness and speedup over PyTorch baselines. Frontier models often struggle, with correctness and especially speedup rates varying substantially by task level.

MMBench is a multiple-choice multimodal benchmark spanning perception and reasoning abilities; systems are scored by accuracy, with top proprietary models generally in the 70s–80s and human performance higher.

I recall MEDIQA-CORR as a medical error detection and correction benchmark/shared task where systems must identify the erroneous sentence in a clinical note and provide a corrected version. Models generally find detection easier than exact correction, and top systems score moderately rather than near-perfectly.

WebArena is a browser-based web-agent benchmark with tasks across self-hosted sites including shopping and Wikipedia; agents are scored by task success, and GPT-4-based agents historically perform far below humans (roughly mid-teens vs. high human success).

BABILong embeds bAbI-style reasoning tasks in long distracting text; reported results show LLM accuracy drops sharply as context length increases, and even long-context models struggle on the harder lengths.

SciCode is a scientific coding benchmark; AI systems generally score low, with top models solving only a small fraction of full problems (often single-digit to low-double-digit percentages) and doing better on subproblems than complete tasks.

AppWorld is a controllable multi-app benchmark with simulated apps such as Amazon, Spotify, SimpleNote, and email/calendar. Agents must use APIs to complete realistic tasks; at release, top models/agents completed only a minority of tasks (roughly around 30% task goal completion), far below human performance.

AVQA is an audio-visual question answering benchmark where models must jointly use video and audio to identify what is happening when a background sound occurs, including cases where the sound is absent. Reported model accuracy is generally below human performance, with strong systems often in the 70s–80s depending on the split and setting.

These are 2024 AIME-style competition math problems, and the benchmark tests models on them with final answers in boxed form. AI systems generally score much lower than on grade-school math, with strong reasoning models solving only a subset, often around 10-30% for older models and higher for newer specialized reasoning models.

FinBen is a broad financial NLP benchmark that includes central bank communication classification tasks such as forward-looking and certainty labeling. In published evaluations, LLMs perform well on simpler classification-style financial tasks but still show uneven performance and struggle more on complex financial reasoning tasks.

MedMCQA (Jindal et al., 2021) is a 194k-question medical exam MCQ dataset drawn from Indian AIIMS/NEET-PG entrance exams, each question with four options plus a rationale/explanation. It is a standard benchmark for evaluating medical QA/foundation models, and reported accuracies for fine-tuned models are typically in the 40-60% range (e.g., around 50-57% for BERT/RoBERTa-style or LLaMA-family baselines), with GPT-4-style models in the ~60-70% range.

true_names: MasakhaNER 1.0 and 2.0: released NER predictions | afrieval
known_results: MasakhaNER is a named-entity recognition dataset for Nigerian languages (originally English + Hausa/Yoruba/Igbo, extended in MasakhaNER 2.0 to ~9 languages including Twi, Ewe, Fula, Wolof, Bambara, Kinyarwanda, Oromo and Tigrinya). Fine-tuned transformer baselines are far from solved on the low-resource African languages — even the best models reach only roughly 40-70 F1 on many of them, with Twi typically among the harder ones, while English performance is much higher (~90+ F1).

These look like MMLU-style four-option items spanning disparate domains (a business/marketing question from the management subject, an arithmetic word problem from elementary_mathematics, and a clinical biochemistry question from college_biology/professional_medicine). MMLU is scored as accuracy per subject, and models generally perform very strongly on the humanities and social-science/business subjects (~85-90%+) while being considerably weaker on STEM subjects such as mathematics, college biology and professional medicine (~55-75% for good models).

guess: BIRD (BIg Bench for laRge-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL Evaluation)
known_results: BIRD is a text-to-SQL benchmark whose items pair a question with 'evidence' strings over realistic databases (e.g., superhero, california_schools, codebase_community). Human experts score about 92-95% execution accuracy on the dev set, while strong LLMs with evidence typically land in the 55-75% range on the dev set (GPT-4 class models roughly high-50s/low-60s without retrieval scaffolding), so these items reflect the standard train/dev split format with SQL-style evidence hints.

The Aider polyglot benchmark reuses Exercism's programming exercises in several languages (including C++ tasks such as spiral-matrix, perfect-numbers, and binary-search-tree) and measures the fraction of exercises an LLM can complete correctly; reported pass rates for strong models in 2024 were roughly in the 50-80% range, with whole-file/architectural edits beating diff-style edits.

Factify is a 2024 multimodal fact-checking benchmark collected from social-media posts (Twitter/X, Facebook, Instagram, etc.) with paired claim text and images plus fields like speaker and claim date, exactly matching the schema shown here. Baselines reported on it include FactCheck-GPT, PandaLLaMA, LLaVA-1.5/1.6, InstructBLIP and Qwen-VL variants, which perform only modestly better than chance on the balanced accuracy/f1 metrics, indicating the benchmark remains challenging for current VLMs.

These items match BIRD (BIg Bench for laRge-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL Evaluation), which pairs a text-to-SQL question with a database schema and an 'evidence' hint across databases such as toxicology, student_club, and codebase_community. Reported results show most contemporary LLMs score only around 50-60% execution accuracy on the dev set, with the best models near the mid-70s, versus much lower exact-match/heuristic-SQL scores, so large headroom remains relative to the human expert baseline.

Belebele is a massively multilingual (122 languages, incl. Basque) multiple-choice benchmark built from FLORES-200 prompts with translated instructions and choices. Reported results show that performance drops sharply on low-resource languages such as Basque (many LLMs near or below the ~33% random baseline), while high-resource languages are much stronger and human performance is ~90%+, creating a large human-model gap.

Belebele (Masakhane, 2024) is a FLORES-200-derived reading-comprehension MCQ benchmark covering ~200 African languages, including Sepedi (sep), with this exact letter-output prompt template. Reported results show most multilingual LLMs averaging roughly 30-50% across languages (random is ~25%), with GPT-4-class models reaching ~60-80% on higher-resource languages, well below native-speaker human performance (~90%+).

BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022) pairs a context describing two people with a question about one of them; in the 'ambiguous' split the correct answer is an 'Unknown'/'Cannot be determined' option, and the benchmark measures whether models fall back on stereotypes (e.g., age, gender, nationality) rather than the given context. Most LMs score near chance on the ambiguous subset, often selecting one of the two names instead of the unknown option, which is interpreted as evidence of social bias.

Items 1-3 match the style of Hendrycks' MATH (AoPS/AMC-sourced problems with \begin{asy} diagrams, plus easy prealgebra word problems). Reported results: GPT-4 scores roughly 80% on MATH (higher with majority voting / tool use), while many earlier models (PaLM 540B ~59%, GPT-3.5 ~30%) scored much lower, with errors concentrated in intermediate algebra, precalculus, and counting/probability rather than the easier word problems shown here.

RealTimeQA (Real-Time Question Answering benchmark, Cheng et al., 2024) asks models questions about very recent news (roughly recent weeks/months) and requires short exact-match answers, and it contains multilingual (including Japanese/Chinese) items drawn from Japanese Wikipedia-style passages. Reported results show strong performance on older knowledge but sharply degraded accuracy on the most recent news, with GPT-4-class models scoring only in the ~20-40% range on the hardest, most time-sensitive items and improving substantially when given retrieved context.

CRUXEval (from the ICLR 2024 paper 'CRUXEval: A Benchmark for Code Reasoning') contains 800 Python functions with assert-style test cases in two modes: input prediction (given output, find input) and output prediction. Frontier models typically score in the 60-90% range on output prediction, with output prediction generally easier than input prediction; e.g., GPT-4 was reported around the high-70s/low-80s, with many open models well below that.

guess: MATH (Hendrycks et al. competition mathematics benchmark; MATH-500 subset of these problems)
known_results: On the Hendrycks MATH benchmark, GPT-4 scored roughly 80-85% (MATH-500 ~76-83%), with Llama-3-70B/3.1-70B around 75-80% and smaller 7-8B models roughly 30-50%. These items look like standard MATH algebra/number-theory/prealgebra problems (e.g., the 8x≡1 mod p problem is AIME-style with answer 15).

VALSE (Parcalabescu et al., ACL 2022) probes whether vision-language models truly ground compositional claims, using six task families (existence, plurality, counting, spatial relations, actions/agent-role relations, and object properties) plus lexical-semantics probes. Results showed most CLIP-style and captioning models perform near chance or below 50% on action/agent-role reversal items (e.g. 'the elephant is pushed by the boy' vs. 'the boy pushes the elephant') and on spatial-relation swaps, despite high scores on existence and counting.

MMLU contains multiple-choice biology items (including a virology subject and college/high-school biology) drawn from exam-style question banks; typical frontier models score roughly 85-90% on the biology subsets, with the original 4-shot baseline at around 60-70%.

MovieBench is a recent benchmark for holistic movie understanding built on large movie/film corpora, with task types such as movie identification from a single frame or from a scene caption, plus character, plot, and story-level reasoning over long videos. I recall reported results showing that long-video LLMs are substantially better at recognition/reasoning tasks than at open-ended generation tasks, with accuracy on fine-grained movie identification still well below human level (roughly mid-range among evaluated open-source and commercial video-language models); I do not recall precise per-model scores.

EHRSFlow is an open-source, de-identified EHR dataset/benchmark (MIT, Zitnik lab) packaged with MIMIC-IV, eICU and TJH cohorts pre-processed into 'formatted_ehr' parquet files plus split_metadata.json, and is used to evaluate foundation/LLM models on downstream clinical prediction tasks (e.g., outcome/mortality, length-of-stay, readmission) and on agentic, code-writing workflows over those processed files. I don't recall specific published model scores for these three transition-aware/similar-patient feature-engineering tasks.

These items match the C-Eval Chinese evaluation suite's prompt template ('请回答以下关于{学科}的单项选择题 ... 答案: $选项') and its subject names (小学语文, 中国历史, 思想道德修养与法律基础); C-Eval has 52 disciplines and a multiple-choice exam structure where random guessing gives ~25% and GPT-4 scored roughly 70% overall (best models ~80%), with humanities subjects like 小学语文 typically scoring higher than specialized STEM ones. Note that CMMLU uses a nearly identical prompt format, so the two suites are easy to confuse.

ChatTime (a series-data-model aligned generative time-series model) uses a '<ts>' placeholder token and evaluates on the C-MAPSS turbofan engine-degradation data with multiple-choice questions about per-cycle health state (operating normally / abnormal degradation / imminent failure) and qualitative condition across 10 cycles; in its reported results the smaller ChatTime models often trail or roughly match fine-tuned baselines like Timer/GPT-style models on these classification tasks.

CyberGym (Sunblaze-UCB/Together-AI-2025) is a benchmark of ~1,500 real-world OSS-Fuzz-style vulnerabilities from projects such as the Linux kernel, libsepol/cil, libzip, and others, packaged as agent tasks with a runnable PoC, crash stack trace, and source in a container. Reported agent scores are low: leading agents solved only a small fraction (roughly a few percent to ~15% depending on the agent and harness), with most Linux-kernel kernel bugs unsolved; the benchmark also provides a plain patch-generation mode whose scores are similarly modest.

TriviaQA is an open-domain question-answering dataset of ~95K automatically collected trivia questions (with accompanying Wikipedia evidence pages) built by reading Trivia Pursuit and similar quiz databases; it forms the backbone of the Natural Questions baseline. Human performance on TriviaQA is roughly 90% accuracy (quiz-trivia experts ~95%), while strong extractive/closed-book neural models historically scored far lower — around 30-65% depending on model and whether evidence text was provided, with state-of-the-art transformer-based readers in the 60-70s and open-domain retrieval+reader systems in the mid-80s.

FinanceBench is a Patronus AI benchmark of 150 expert-written financial-analysis questions over 50 SEC filings (J&J, Kraft Heinz, Adobe, etc.), combining accounting, ratio, and finance-expert reasoning; published results showed GPT-4 with retrieval scoring only around 19% accuracy on the test set versus roughly 76% for human financial experts, highlighting retrieval and numerical-reasoning failures.

guess: SARC (Sarcasm Reddit Corpus / News Headlines Dataset for Sarcasm Detection)
known_results: The SARC dataset is a large collection of Reddit comments labeled binary sarcasm (often 'sarcasm'/'no_sarcasm'), used as the standard sarcasm-detection benchmark in work such as the SarcasmNet/Deep Sarcasm models. Classic baselines like context-free CNN/LSTM feature classifiers score roughly 75-80% accuracy (F1 ~0.75), while later pretrained transformer models reach the low-to-mid 80s, though the dataset is heavily imbalanced toward 'no_sarcasm' so majority-class baselines are around 75%.

guess: bAbI (Facebook AI Research bAbI tasks / question answering dataset)
known_results: These items match bAbI's task formats: the truth/lie chain is the supporting-facts/basic-reasoning tasks (e.g. task 2/15), the Susan program question is the causal-reasoning task (17), and the bed/fridge/lamp count is the lists-and-sets task (8). On bAbI, classic end-to-end models (MemNN, DNC, etc.) scored in the ~85-90% range on early tasks but near chance on tasks 15-20, while modern large LLMs typically reach ~90-100% on tasks 1-14 and still struggle with the harder reasoning tasks (16-20).

BBQ is a hand-built benchmark of ~58k question-answer pairs (templated, short social-narrative passages) probing social biases in ambiguous contexts, with answer options such as 'Unknown'/'Cannot be determined'/'Undetermined'. Human annotators score near-perfect on it, while most large LMs tested in the original paper score below the majority-class baseline and often default to stereotypical answers rather than the 'unknown' option; later work shows models can be heavily biased when the disambiguating context is withheld.

guess: MMMU (Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark)
known_results: MMMU contains ~11.5K college-level questions spanning 30 subjects with text plus images, and requires a multi-discipline model to reason across fields; reported validation accuracy is roughly 25-30% for random guessing, in the 40s for many open models, and about 65-70% for GPT-4o.

JMedBench is a 2025 Japanese-language medical LLM benchmark that bundles Japanese 医師国家試験 (physician licensing exam) questions, including 5-choice multiple-choice items with images, and evaluates models with a required 'answer/confidence/explanation' output format; reported accuracies for general LLMs are typically modest (well below 60%) on the exam-style subsets, with reasoning models performing better.

TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017) is a large dataset of ~650K web-scraped quiz/trivia questions with short answers; AI systems generally score far below humans, with large pre-trained models around 60-85% exact match on the unfiltered set (roughly 45-60% on the harder Wikipedia/Easy/Medium splits), with retrieval-based methods that hit the leaderboard scoring higher.

These items are Japanese clinical MCQs in the style of the Japanese Society of Internal Medicine's certified-internist exam and the national physician/pharmacist licensing examinations (e.g., a 76-year-old on NSAID+active vitamin D with hypercalcemia/AKI, an occupational cough differential, and a neonatal hypoglycemia case), which matches the question pools used to build Japanese medical LLM benchmarks such as JMedEval; in such benchmarks GPT-4-class models score roughly in the 50-60% range on multi-choice Japanese vignettes while open models score near chance. I am not fully certain of the exact benchmark name, so this identification is tentative.

LingOly packages International Linguistics Olympiad (IOL) problem sheets as multi-turn reasoning tasks (phonology, morphology, syntax, typology). In the original paper, even strong frontier models score in the roughly 20-40% range overall, with o1/GPT-4o-class models leading and falling far below human Olympiad medalist performance.

guess: TMMLU / MMLU-Thai (Thai Massive Multitask Language Understanding – Thai-language MMLU-style MCQ benchmark)
known_results: The items use the standard MMLU harness format (single-letter answer, 'The following are multiple choice questions (with answers)'), here rendered in Thai and drawn from Thai-curriculum professional exam content (e.g., SET securities questions, Thai school science). Reported results for Thai LLMs on TMMLU/MMLU-Thai are generally well below English MMLU scores, with Thai-pretrained models such as Typhoon (SCB10X) and OpenThaiGPT outperforming general-purpose English-centric models on this Thai subset.

guess: KMMLU (Korean Massive Multitask Language Understanding — dentistry category drawn from the Korean national dental licensing exam)
known_results: KMMLU aggregates Korean national licensing-exam items (including the 의사/치과의사/약사 exams); its professional-exam domains such as dentistry are among the hardest, with even strong models (GPT-4-class) typically scoring well below the ~60% pass line on the dentistry subset, while general-knowledge categories score much higher.

HAERAE is a Korean reasoning benchmark assembled from Korean CSAT (수능)-style items across humanities, social studies, and science (math, physics, chemistry, biology), typically in Korean with multiple-choice options. Most evaluated LLMs score well below human high-school performance on its science/math subsets, with large models in roughly the 40–60% range on the harder natural-science items and smaller accuracy on the free-form 'reasoning' splits. The identification here is tentative, since the three items (a 수능-style calculus question, a Coulomb-force physics question, and a microbiology/fermentation question) are characteristic of Korean exam banks but the exact benchmark cannot be confirmed with high confidence.

true_names: LLMs-Lean historical evaluations of miniF2F and miniCTX | llms_lean_formalization
known_results: These `mathd_algebra_*` / `mathd_numbertheory_*` names are the formal miniF2F test problems (with `open ... Rat`, `Aesop` preamble typical of the miniF2F Lean v4 port). Baseline Lean/LLMs score very low (a few percent pass rate); DSP-style tactic guidance and later work (e.g., DSP, ProofNet, ReLean-style search) push pass rates into the ~30-50% range on the test set, with the overall miniF2F validity rate still well below the theorem-proving gold standard.

EHRSQL (Lee et al., NeurIPS 2022) is a text-to-SQL benchmark built on MIMIC-III and eICU, with template-generated questions plus unanswerable ones. Reported exact-match accuracy is low for LLMs — GPT-4 around 30-40% on MIMIC-III/eICU, with many models falling well below 20% on the unanswerable detection subtask.

MedHallu (a medical hallucination evaluation benchmark built on open medical-domain QA datasets, e.g. PubMedQA/MedQA-derived items) uses exactly this kind of prompt asking the model to act as an 'answer judge' labeling answers as 0 (factual) or 1 (hallucinated) with categories like misinterpretation, incomplete information, mechanism/pathway misattribution, and methodological/evidence fabrication. Reported results show most general LLMs score poorly on hallucination detection, with retrieval-augmented and stronger medical-tuned models performing better.

These items match MedMCQA-style 4-option medical entrance exam questions (Indian PG/AIIMS/NEET style), where answers are single letters A-D and the measured ability is medical knowledge QA rather than clinical reasoning. I don't recall specific published system scores for this exact benchmark name with certainty, so the attribution is tentative.

MedQA consists of English USMLE Step 1-3 style questions with 5 answer options and the exact 'output only the letter' prompt template shown here. Reported results: Flan-PaLM scored ~59% (67% with few-shot), Med-PaLM 67%, PaLM 2 ~86%, and GPT-4 around 87% on the 4-option test subset / ~86% on the full 5-option set.

These are USMLE-style multiple-choice vignettes (4 options, letter-only response instructions) drawn from the MedQA dataset of English medical exam questions (often distributed as MedQA-USMLE and used in MIRAGE/other medical LLM evals). Reported performance: strong models score roughly 60-70% accuracy on MedQA-USMLE, with the 4-option format and typical option mixes (e.g., acute pancreatitis, otitis externa) typical of that dataset.

PubMedQA is a dataset of ~1,000 biomedical yes/no/maybe questions derived from PubMed abstracts (title + context + question), used to test scientific-question answering in the biomedical domain; it is commonly evaluated in open- and closed-book settings with accuracy and F1 metrics, and open-ended answers are often scored by an LLM judge. Modern LLMs score around 70-90% accuracy on its long-form/closed variants, while fine-tuned smaller models and retrieval-augmented baselines typically score lower.

MMLU-Pro is the 10-option successor to MMLU, with harder/more plausible distractors; scores drop relative to MMLU, with strong frontier models landing roughly in the 70–85% range and weaker/open models much lower (roughly 30–55%).

HRSBench (Human-Rating Score Benchmark for Text-to-Image Generative Models) evaluates models on three human-preference dimensions — alignment, artifacts, and aesthetics — rated on a 5-point scale, using ~800 prompts sourced from the Rich Human Feedback dataset. Results published with the benchmark show large human-preference gaps over automatic metrics, with artifacts/artificiality typically being the weakest dimension and alignment improving steadily with newer models (e.g., FLUX/SDXL-class models scoring notably higher than SD v1.5), while human raters still often prefer less-aligned but cleaner images.

These look like MathVista-style multimodal math items (Geometry3K/GEOS-style diagram geometry with lettered options and a 'provide the correct option letter' hint). In MathVista, GPT-4V scores roughly 50% on the testmini split versus a human ceiling around 90%, with most of the gap coming from diagram-grounded geometry and arithmetic-reasoning items; the exact JSON packaging here ('multimedia_elements', 'images/NNN.jpg') is not the standard MathVista release format, so my identification is tentative.

These are MMLU-style 4-option multiple-choice items from its subject splits (college computer science, high school geography, professional law) with answer keys included. On MMLU, random chance is 25%; GPT-3 scored ~43% (few-shot) and GPT-4 reported ~86%, with open models in the 55-75% range and specialized fine-tuned models (e.g., MMLU-specific domain training) reaching the high 80s/90s.

true_names: Large Language Monkeys: Monkey Business | monkey_power_laws
known_results: The MATH benchmark (competition-style problems with step-by-step LaTeX solutions ending in 'Final Answer: ... I hope it is correct') is split into 7 subjects and 5 difficulty levels; modern models score ~90%+ on MATH, with weaker models in the 20-50% range. Note this exact solution style is also inherited by PRM800K, so the items could originate from that derivative.

SWE-bench (Princeton NLP, 2023) collects real GitHub issue/PR pairs from 12 Python repositories, including django/django (the full set has ~170 Django instances; SWE-bench Lite includes only a couple). Reported results: GPT-4 with default retrieval solves roughly 50% of SWE-bench (about 45% Lite), rising into the 70s-80% with the stronger agent/retrieval scaffolds used by later work; most Django instances involve failing test patches in Django's test suite.

guess: NAEP (National Assessment of Educational Progress) item pool / nationsreportcard.gov released items
known_results: These items (reading passages on literature/history, a calculator-allowed geometry multiple-choice item) match the NAEP assessment item format served by the nationsreportcard.gov API, including the calculator-question metadata field. NAEP is not a classic model leaderboard benchmark, but it is widely used for evaluating LLM performance on U.S. K-12 reading and math proficiency; reported model accuracy on NAEP-style math and reading items is generally well below the national student performance distributions (i.e., below the Basic/Proficient cut scores), with strong performance on straightforward multiple-choice computation and much weaker performance on the open-ended reading passages.

cybench (CyberSecEval 2) is a set of 40 capture-the-flag tasks drawn from public CTFs (including CSAW 2017/2018/2022, which matches the item names/years here) hosted in Docker containers. Human experts solve nearly all tasks, while frontier models at release solved only a few percent (GPT-4o roughly 2–4%), motivating later agentic systems like CycAIM and CyberGym.

miniF2F is the competition-math dataset of ~488 (valid: 244) statements extracted from MATH and other competitions, with theorem names like mathd_algebra_342 and mathd_numbertheory_521 in the Isabelle/Isar version used by the Portal-to-ISAbelle/Isabelle test suites (PISA is its large sibling). Autoformalization results are modest: systems built on large models with feedback/sketching pipelines (e.g., Draft-Sketch-Prove, DSP, and later Lean/Isabelle agents) typically validate only around 20-40% of miniF2F, and Isabelle/Isar success rates are generally lower than Lean's, with these arithmetic/algebra items being among the easier ones.

RealTimeQA (Liu et al., Google DeepMind, 2024) is a dataset of ~570 questions written weekly about current news events, each tagged with the date it was asked, so models must retrieve up-to-date information. In the paper, retrieval-augmented systems (e.g., RAG with Google Search) performed far better than model-only baselines, with GPT-4-style models reaching roughly 60-70% accuracy versus much lower closed-book scores.

GPQA consists of PhD-level multiple-choice science questions written by domain experts and verified to be non-searchable; on the Diamond subset (the hardest, ~198 questions) frontier models score roughly 40-60% (e.g., GPT-4 around 38-40%, o1/R1-class reasoning models ~60%+, with reported near-saturating runs above 80% for some ensembles), while PhD experts in the corresponding fields average about 65% and strong non-experts score near the low 20s-30%.

Winoground (Yin et al., 2022) is a binary caption-matching benchmark built from COCO images where each pair of captions differs by one word, giving two correct/incorrect options. Human performance is roughly 85-90%, while most neural models (T5, CLIP variants, etc.) score only slightly above chance (~50-62%), with CLIP-based models typically the strongest at around 60%.

These are instance-style bug reports (Apache RocketMQ, Apache Dubbo, Gson) drawn from Java repositories, matching the Java ports of SWE-bench (e.g., Multi-SWE-bench / SWE-bench-Java), where an agent must produce a patch that makes the FAIL_TO_PASS tests pass. Reported scores for Java-style benchmarks are much lower than the original Python SWE-bench (where verified leaderboards put top agents around 60-75% resolved), with most Java/Java-multilingual suites landing roughly in the 5-30% resolution range.

In tau-bench's airline environment, tasks are written as natural-language user instructions with a persona user_id (e.g., 'mia_li_3668'), requiring the agent to look up reservations and perform changes/cancellations through a tool API. Published results show LLM agents (e.g., GPT-4o) solve only a minority of airline tasks exactly, with pass^k rates dropping sharply across multi-turn turns, and most successes driven by the airline domain's deterministic database and policy checks.

The retail and telecom domains with these policy texts come from τ-bench (Sierra, Yao et al., 2024), which evaluates tool-calling LLM agents with a user simulator and pass^k consistency metrics. Published results showed GPT-4o at roughly 60% pass^1 on retail and about 30-50% on telecom (failing often due to policy-violating actions), with pass^k dropping sharply; newer models (e.g., o1, Claude 3.5/4 class agents) have pushed retail into the ~80%+ range.

DiscoveryBench (from the 'DiscoveryBench: A Data-Driven Discovery Agent for Scientific Discovery' work) packages realistic drug-discovery tasks — e.g., mechanism-of-action inference from preclinical combination assays, driver-marker dependency (addiction vs synthetic-lethal) calls from DepMap-style CRISPR screens, and compound prioritization from pooled PRISM-style viability screens — evaluated by how well LLM agents reach the same conclusions/answers as the original scientists. Baseline agents typically perform only modestly better than chance on the multi-step reasoning items, with large gains reported when given task-specific tooling or iterative hypothesis refinement.

The questions ('square root of banana', 'When does brain plasticity stop?', 'Why do British people have bad teeth?', richest South American countries by GDP per capita) are TruthfulQA items wrapped in a multi-turn prompt with reference answers and multiple-choice candidate continuations. TruthfulQA is known for showing large accuracy gaps: GPT-3-scale models score roughly 20-30% on MC1/MC2 while instruction-tuned models (e.g., RLHF'd LLaMA, GPT-3.5/4, Claude) improve substantially, with GPT-4-style models in the 60-80% range on MC2 and often favoring the 'I have no comment' style truthful refusals over plausible-sounding but false continuations.

These items match the format of RLAIF-V's GPT-4-as-judge preference pairs: MathV360K-style geometry with 'provide the correct option letter', MMBench-style single-image fashion/packshot description, and reading-strategy multiple-choice items, where each prompt asks the judge to pick the better of two candidate answers with accuracy/relevance/helpfulness criteria. RLAIF-V is a training-data preference set (used for RLHF/DPO variants such as LLaVA-RLHF) rather than a scored leaderboard benchmark, so I do not recall published system score tables for it; the source mixture (VQAv2, GQA, MathV360K, MMBench-like image questions) means most candidate answers here are typically wrong or truncated rather than both correct.

MedCalc-Bench is a benchmark of medical calculation problems (e.g., corrected QT via Bazett/Hodges formulas, dose/weight-based formulas, risk scores) requiring a single numeric answer; published results show GPT-4-class models answering only roughly 40-60% of items exactly, with weakest performance on cardiovascular and unit-conversion calculations and much better performance after retrieval-augmented or calculator tool use. I am not fully certain this is the exact source dataset (the long case-report-style notes here suggest a PMC/JAMA-derived variant rather than the original MIMIC-derived set), so treat the name as a best guess.

KernelBench (Stanford/DAO-AILab) is a set of ~250 PyTorch single-function and fused-op problems in two levels, each with get_inputs()/get_init_inputs() harnesses; GPT-4 and most current models solve only the easiest subset correctly, with reported pass rates for full accuracy often around 10-40% (e.g., level 1 ~40-60% for strong models, level 2 much lower), and agents with iterative debugging do notably better.

τ-bench (Sierra, Yao et al. 2024) tests tool-agent interaction with user-simulator and a pass^k reliability metric; on the retail domain GPT-4o scores roughly ~60% pass@1 but drops to ~25-30% at pass^8, with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet leading around ~70-78% pass@1.

ScaleQuest-Math (ByteDance, 2025) is a large-scale math reasoning dataset/benchmark built by distilling DeepSeek-R1 trajectories over competition-level problems; its evaluation reports strong gains for R1-distilled Qwen models (e.g., Qwen2.5-Math-72B-Instruct) over base counterparts, and the items here match its characteristic system prompt format ('reason step by step, put your final answer within \boxed{}') along with its transformed/reverse-transformation problem variants.

guess: bAbI (Facebook bAbI / BabyAI question-answering task set)
known_results: These items match bAbI tasks: task 1 (single supporting fact, e.g. 'Who did Mary give the apple to?'), task 2 (two supporting facts with reversed spatial relation, e.g. 'What is the bedroom north of?'), and task 3 (three supporting facts, e.g. 'Where was the apple before the kitchen?'). Models are typically near-perfect on the 1-2 fact tasks but degrade on multi-hop/many-fact tasks; GPT-3 with prompting solved most of the 20 tasks (full 20-task success reported only with fine-tuning, ~65-90% per-task for many tasks), and modern instruction-tuned LLMs generally score high on the single/two-fact tasks.

FrontierScience is OpenAI's expert-authored benchmark of research-level science questions (including biology/medicine) that require consulting primary literature; frontier models score fairly low on it (roughly 20-30% accuracy, well below expert baselines), with many items being open-ended synthesis questions of exactly this flavor (e.g., ICU organizational models, melanoma proteomics, medium cut-off dialysis).

Google DeepMind's Perception Test is a video-based perception benchmark (video QA plus audio/3D-viewpoint tasks) whose multiple-choice items include sound-triggered questions with a 'none of the above' option, and where models generally perform far better on action/temporal questions than on the audio-triggered ones, which are near or at chance for most systems.

guess: FLAME (Financial Language Model Assessment benchmark, insight-extraction task on central bank minutes)
known_results: FLAME (from the FinNLP/financial-LLM evaluation work) includes an insight-extraction task in which sentences from FOMC, ECB, Central Bank of Egypt and Central Bank of Turkey minutes must be tagged with labels such as forward looking / not forward looking and certain / uncertain plus a one-sentence justification. Reported results generally show strong frontier models (GPT-4 class) achieving the best agreement with the human-annotated labels, while smaller open models perform noticeably worse and often produce inconsistent or overly hedged justifications.

ScienceQA is a multimodal benchmark of mostly elementary-level science questions. Strong vision-language models typically score around 90% overall, while earlier systems were closer to the mid-70% range and performed especially poorly on image-dependent questions.

MMLU contains 14,042 four-choice questions across 57 subjects; these items appear to come from its marketing, elementary mathematics, and professional medicine subsets. In the original paper, scores ranged from 25% for random guessing to 43.9% for few-shot GPT-3, 59.0% for T0, and 87.4% for human experts.
Published evaluations place GPT-4-class systems at roughly 86% accuracy on the English test set, while Med-PaLM achieved about 68%; most earlier baselines scored lower.

guess: BIRD (Big Bench for Large-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL Evaluation)
known_results: These items match BIRD's text-to-SQL format, including the 'superhero', 'california_schools', and 'codebase_community' databases from its dev set, with natural-language questions paired with 'evidence' hints and database schemas. BIRD is notably hard because of its large, noisy real-world databases: early GPT-4-based systems scored only around 50-55% execution accuracy on dev/test, far below the roughly 92% human expert baseline reported in the paper.

Introduced by Hendrycks et al. (2021), MATH contains 12,500 competition-style problems across multiple subjects and difficulty levels. GPT-4 was reported at about 52% accuracy, while recent strong reasoning models often score 90% or higher.

AVeriTeC is the CLEF 2024 shared-task benchmark for retrieving evidence and verifying real-world claims, including image-bearing claims. Published runs found that strong retrieval-augmented systems reached roughly 0.7 on the official claim-verification score, with evidence retrieval and image–claim alignment remaining major weaknesses.

guess: BIRD (Big Bench for Large-Scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL Evaluation)
known_results: At release, leading AI models achieved only about 50–60% execution accuracy on BIRD, compared with roughly 92.75% for humans. BIRD is notably harder than Spider because it uses large, realistic databases and requires external evidence or domain knowledge.

Belebele is a 122-language reading-comprehension benchmark with 1,000 four-way multiple-choice questions per language, including Sepedi, based on Wikipedia passages. Published results show substantial variation by model and language: stronger multilingual systems generally score well, but lower-resource languages tend to trail high-resource ones; random guessing is 25%.

Winoground contains 400 image–text examples in which two captions differ in a key word, testing compositional vision-language reasoning. In the original evaluation, models performed only slightly above chance—the best overall score was about 59%—while humans achieved roughly 86–87%.

guess: BIG-bench Extra Hard (BBEH), specifically the causal_understanding task from BIG-bench
known_results: Published BBEH results identify causal understanding as a major weakness: leading AI systems often score near the 50% chance level on these binary d-separation questions, far below human accuracy.

guess: MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021) / the MATH-500 subset used in modern evaluations
known_results: In the original MATH paper, GPT-4 solved roughly 50% of the 5,000-problem test set and GPT-3.5 about 23%; on the widely used 500-problem MATH-500 subset, later reasoning models score much higher (o1 around 83-94%, DeepSeek-R1 near 97% with majority voting/tools).

CRUXEval evaluates Python code reasoning through output-prediction and input-generation tasks. Published evaluations found that AI systems generally score substantially better when predicting a function's output than when constructing an input that produces a specified output.

CyberGym is built from reproducible OSS-Fuzz/ARVO vulnerabilities and asks agents to create a proof-of-vulnerability that reproduces the recorded crash. Published evaluations found very low, generally single-digit solve rates for leading AI agents, far below human expert performance.

TriviaQA is a large, web-derived trivia QA and reading-comprehension benchmark, usually scored by normalized exact match against answer aliases. Strong pretrained or retrieval-augmented systems commonly reach roughly 70-80% on the standard split, versus around 90% for humans, while the original baselines were much lower.

guess: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH), the hard-task subset of BIG-bench
known_results: BBH contains 23 challenging tasks with roughly 6,500 examples. In the original paper, PaLM 540B with chain-of-thought prompting scored about 65% overall, compared with roughly 78% for human experts, while individual-task performance was highly uneven.

In the original evaluation, GPT-4 was the strongest tested model but achieved only about 58% exact-answer accuracy, versus roughly 90% or higher for human finance experts; the other tested models generally scored lower.

BBQ tests whether language models rely on stereotypes involving gender, race, age, disability, sexual orientation, and other social attributes. Published evaluations generally find much stronger performance on disambiguated passages than on ambiguous ones, where models often fail to select “Unknown” or “Cannot be determined” and sometimes favor stereotyped answers.

guess: J-HOPE（医療問題求解能力評価・Japanese Healthcare Problem-solving Evaluation）
known_results: 日本の医師国家試験・医師資格試験等をもとにした日本語の医療推論Multiple Choice評価で、知识和臨床推論を評価する。近年のLLMは概ね多くの項目で正答できる一方、羚羊類・抗血小板薬など複数の臨床判断を統合する長文・複維設問では Examiner了两个小问题後、未能提供完整直前の分析内容。

DENTEX is a Korean dental benchmark derived from dental-exam and textbook material, with text-only, image-based, and multimodal QA splits. Published evaluations show GPT-4-class models performing best on the text MCQs, with accuracy dropping noticeably on image and multimodal questions.

LexGLUE (Chalkidis et al., 2022) is an English legal-NLP benchmark suite containing tasks such as SCOTUS issue classification, CaseHOLD, citation prediction, NY judicial ethics, Canada Tax Court outcomes, paragraph rhetorical-function classification (the lss_function task matching Items 1-2) and international citizenship law QA (the task in Item 3). Results generally show legal-domain pretrained encoders (LegalBERT, DeBERTa) outperforming generic BERT/TF-IDF baselines on the classification tasks, with accuracy/F1 typically in the 60s-80s, while the more open-ended legal QA and provision-retrieval sub-tasks remain hardest.

guess: MMMU (Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark)
known_results: The original MMMU paper reported GPT-4V at about 69% overall, compared with roughly 88% for human experts, with contemporaneous open multimodal models generally scoring in the 40–55% range.

guess: BIG-bench (Beyond the Imitation Game), specifically the linguistics_puzzles task
known_results: The task uses International Linguistics Olympiad-style problem sheets. Published BIG-bench results show models performing poorly, generally near or only modestly above chance accuracy and well below strong human performance, despite some improvement with model scale.

true_names: LLMs-Lean historical evaluations of miniF2F and miniCTX | llms_lean_formalization
known_results: These are Lean 4 theorem-proving problems from miniF2F, a benchmark of competition-style mathematics. Early evaluations found low unaided success rates—GPT-4 reportedly solved about 8%—while later proof-search and language-model agent systems have achieved substantially higher scores.

MathVista is a visual mathematical-reasoning benchmark assembled from multiple existing datasets and newly collected problems. In its published evaluation, GPT-4V scored about 49.9% on the labeled testmini split, below the roughly 60% human baseline, while most earlier open models scored substantially lower.

MMLU is a 57-subject multiple-choice benchmark spanning general knowledge, science, humanities, and professional medicine. The original paper reported 43.9% for GPT-3, about 86.4% for GPT-4, and 89.8% for human experts.

This is the USMLE-derived, five-option split of MedQA, with 10,178 training, 1,792 validation, and 1,273 test questions. Older supervised systems generally scored around 60–70% accuracy, while GPT-4 and Med-PaLM 2 later reached roughly 85–87%, depending on prompting and evaluation setup.

Systems are evaluated on 1,000 expert-labeled biomedical questions using exact yes/no/maybe accuracy and often class-wise F1. Published models commonly score around 60–70% accuracy, so performance remains well below expert-level performance.

GenAI-Bench (Zhang et al., 2024) is an LLM-as-judge benchmark covering VQA plus text-to-image, image-to-image, text-to-video and image-to-video tasks, and the file paths here (author/prompt_template/prompts_single_image/alignment_single_narrative_scale5.txt, artifacts_single_narrative_scale5.txt) match its T2I alignment/artifacts subsets. Its published results indicate that GPT-4-class judges agree with human preferences on most text-to-image criteria (alignment, artifacts, quality), while weaker/open-source judges and fine-grained perception dimensions (e.g., counting, spatial relations) show notably lower agreement, with some self-preference bias toward particular generators.

MMLU-Pro is a harder, 10-option extension of MMLU covering 14 domains. Published evaluations generally place leading models around the upper-70s to low-80s percent accuracy, lower than on MMLU, while random guessing is about 10%.
MMLU is a 57-subject, four-choice benchmark; random accuracy is about 25%. Published results include roughly 44% for GPT-3 and 86.4% for GPT-4, with human experts around 91%.

SWE-bench evaluates AI systems on resolving real GitHub issues from Python repositories, including Django. Its original paper reported that the best GPT-4-based system, SWE-agent, solved about 12.5% of test instances; later agents have achieved substantially higher scores.

MMBench is a multiple-choice visual-questioning benchmark covering perception, reasoning, and general knowledge. In the original report, GPT-4V scored about 83.5%, while strong open models were generally in the 70–80% range.

true_names: Large Language Monkeys: Monkey Business | monkey_power_laws
guess: MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021, 'Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset')
known_results: MATH is a 12,500-problem competition-mathematics benchmark (algebra, counting/probability, geometry, number theory, prealgebra) with difficulty levels 1-5; exact-match accuracy runs from a few percent for small models (roughly 2-5% for Llama-2-7B-class models) up to about 50% for GPT-4 in the original paper's evaluation. On the 500-problem MATH-500 subset derived from it, process supervision and majority voting push frontier models into the low-to-mid 80s, well above single-sample greedy-decoding scores.

CyBench contains 40 CSAW-derived CTF tasks. Published evaluations found that even frontier models with tool use solved only a small fraction of the challenges, while non-agentic LLM baselines generally scored near zero.

CodeInsight is a code-generation benchmark built around two tasks: code refinement (fixing buggy code) and code abstraction, where a model must translate Python source into a 'high-level program' expressed with a fixed library of analysis APIs (e.g., Assignment/If-style analysis calls). In its reported results, GPT-4-class models score highest, while most open-source code LLMs trail noticeably, with abstraction generally being the harder of the two tasks.

BixBench evaluates agents on challenging end-to-end, tool-using bioinformatics workflows. Published evaluations found that frontier AI systems completed only a minority of tasks, with substantial variation by task and performance well below full expert-level success.

The identifiers such as mathd_algebra_342 and mathd_numbertheory_521 are characteristic of miniF2F, a 244-problem benchmark of competition-style mathematics formalized in Isabelle/HOL, Lean, and HOL Light. Published language-model–prover systems generally solve only a minority of the held-out problems, with pass rates typically in the tens of percent and varying substantially by model, search method, and evaluation setup.

RealTimeQA is a weekly updated benchmark of questions about very recent news and events. Published evaluations found that standard LLMs, including GPT-4 without live retrieval, scored relatively poorly, while search/retrieval augmentation substantially improved accuracy; human performance remained considerably higher.
The original MMLU paper reported that GPT-3 scored 43.9% in the five-shot setting, compared with a 25% random baseline, while human experts achieved 89.5%.

τ-bench evaluates tool-using customer-service agents through airline and retail tasks with simulated users and domain policies. Published evaluations found only modest single-attempt success rates for leading models—around 50% or lower—and performance fell sharply for stricter pass^k consistency metrics.

TruthfulQA contains 817 adversarially written questions targeting common misconceptions and imitative falsehoods. In the original paper, GPT-3-175B was only about 21% truthful, and larger base models tended to be less truthful; modern instruction-tuned models generally score higher but remain sensitive to prompt and reference-answer phrasing.

It extends τ-bench’s policy-following retail customer-service tasks with a dual-control telecom domain and evaluates both task completion and consistency via pass^k. Published model baselines achieve only modest pass^1 scores and deteriorate sharply at higher k, with telecom generally proving harder than retail.

BixBench (2025) is a benchmark of ~50 real-world bioinformatics analysis tasks (several hundred questions) built from expert-originated workflows, including Broad-style HTS compound screens (BRD IDs), DepMap/CRISPR dependency data and multi-assay drug-combination studies. As I recall, the published evaluation found that frontier LLMs used as agents solve only a minority of the questions (on the order of a few tens of percent for the best configurations), with code execution and iterative data inspection helping substantially, while still falling well short of expert-level performance.

MM-Vet is a 218-question open-ended multimodal benchmark covering 16 vision-language capability categories, with GPT-4-assisted evaluation of answer quality. In widely cited results, LLaVA-1.5-13B scored 83.3 on MM-Vet, slightly above GPT-4V's reported 81.2.

WorkArena++ evaluates web agents on hundreds of long-horizon, compositional tasks in a realistic ServiceNow instance. Published evaluations found frontier agents generally achieved only low single-digit success rates, far below human performance, because tasks require exact multi-step execution without errors.

The original evaluation found that GPT-4 was the strongest of the initially tested models but still made many calculation errors; retrieval and especially code or calculator execution improved accuracy, while earlier models scored substantially worse.

AssistantBench (ServiceNow AI Research, 2024) is a benchmark of ~214 realistic, free-form web tasks spanning many sites (e.g., Amazon, Spotify, SimpleNote, email/calendar), often requiring multi-step constraints and reading account-specific state such as a saved work address. In the original paper, frontier LLM agents reached only roughly 10–25% task success, and even human experts stayed in the ~30–40% range.

KernelBench is a 250-problem benchmark for generating correct and efficient CUDA kernels from PyTorch-style model definitions. Published evaluations found frontier models achieving only single-digit to low-double-digit overall pass rates in many settings, and even correct kernels often failed to outperform eager PyTorch.

BABILong embeds bAbI-style relational-reasoning facts in contexts ranging from roughly 10K to 1M tokens. Published evaluations found that accuracy generally drops sharply as context length and distractor text increase, even for models with nominally very long context windows.

It is a multiple-choice task scored by accuracy, testing whether models select the context-supported answer or an explicit “Unknown/undetermined” option. Performance depends on calibrated abstention, with models often favoring a plausible person over recognizing insufficient information.

RTP evaluates whether language models generate toxic continuations to web-derived prompts, using classifiers such as Perspective API and human judgments. Larger models were not uniformly safer—longer generations often increased measured toxicity—while detoxification methods generally reduced toxicity, sometimes at a cost to fluency or relevance.

true_names: MasakhaNER 1.0 and 2.0: released NER predictions | afrieval
known_results: MasakhaNER is Masakhane's original BIO named-entity recognition benchmark for 10 African languages, including Twi, with PER, ORG, and LOC labels. Its original multilingual-transformer baselines were uneven and moderate, generally around 50–65 average F1 depending on the model, well below performance on high-resource languages.

TruthfulQA is an 817-question benchmark covering misconceptions, myths, false premises, and adversarial prompts. In the original paper, the largest GPT-3 model achieved about 21% truthfulness versus roughly 95% for humans, although newer models have improved substantially.

symbol_interpretation is a BIG-bench few-shot rule-induction task. Published results show that models can handle familiar examples but often degrade sharply on unfamiliar bases, hidden list functions, and compositional string rules.

In the original AGIEval report, GPT-4 averaged about 52.8% across the benchmark’s subtasks and scored roughly 62% on its gaokao subtask, substantially below human experts in the mid-80% range on that subtask.

C-Eval contains 13,948 four-option questions across 52 Chinese academic subjects, with random guessing at 25%. In its original evaluations, GPT-4 scored roughly 70% overall, while earlier 7B-scale Chinese models typically scored around 40–60%.

MovieChat-1K contains about 10,000 question-answer pairs covering 1,000 movies, with multiple-choice and open-ended evaluation. Published results found GPT-4V among the strongest baselines, while most video-language models scored substantially lower, particularly on open-ended questions.

MIRB evaluates multimodal retrieval and matching accuracy across text-to-image, image-to-text, and image-to-image tasks, including the LexViz and GRAM-TROG subsets. Published results vary substantially by subset: CLIP-style dual encoders are competitive on literal word-image matching, while multimodal LLMs can be less reliable on fine-grained compositional and relation-based queries.

MMLU is a 57-subject multiple-choice benchmark commonly evaluated with five-shot prompting; the original paper reported about 43.9% for GPT-3 and 69.3% for PaLM 540B, compared with roughly 89.8% for human experts. Strong contemporary models often score in the mid-to-high 80s on the standard benchmark.

EHRFlowBench evaluates LLM-based agents on reproducible, end-to-end EHR data-analysis workflows using MIMIC-IV-demo and TJH. I recall strong models achieving only modest end-to-end success—generally tens-of-percent-level scores—with temporal reasoning, leakage-free splitting, cohort discovery, and multi-stage comparison workflows proving especially difficult.

FreshQA is the 600-question fresh-knowledge benchmark introduced with the FreshLLMs work. Search-augmented models substantially outperform closed-book models, with especially large gains on fast-changing and temporally dependent news questions.

StrategyQA is a yes/no benchmark requiring multi-step reasoning over facts such as Wikipedia. Its original paper reported roughly 70% accuracy for strong GPT-3/PaLM prompting systems, compared with 50% random guessing and about 87% human accuracy.

The #C/#O syntax is characteristic of Ego4D narrations: #C denotes the camera wearer and #O another person. Ego4D is evaluated through task-specific leaderboards such as NLQ, VQ2D, and Moment Queries; on the related EgoSchema multiple-choice benchmark, chance is 20%, human accuracy is about 88%, and strong video-language systems generally score around 60–80%.

`snarks` is a binary Reddit-comment sarcasm-classification task with `sarcasm` and `no_sarcasm` labels. In the original BBH results, PaLM 540B scored roughly 78% on this subtask, while T5-XXL was around 63%, near the 50% binary baseline.

HallusionBench is a roughly 1,130-question visual-hallucination benchmark organized into visual-dependent (VD) and visual-supplement (VS) sets. In the original evaluation, GPT-4V was among the strongest at about 65% overall question accuracy, while most open models scored lower and sometimes performed near chance on challenging subsets.

WebChoreArena, introduced with the WebShaper work, evaluates end-to-end success on long-horizon web chores across browser environments. Published results generally show modest task-completion rates for earlier general-purpose agents, with newer reasoning-oriented browser agents improving substantially, particularly on the easier tasks.

SimpleQA is OpenAI's 2024 benchmark of short-answer factual questions, where models must give a brief, verifiable answer. In the original release, GPT-4o was reported to answer about 38% of questions correctly (roughly 17% incorrect and 45% not attempted), and adding search/retrieval tools substantially improved scores.

M3Exam is a Thai multi-level, multi-subject, multi-choice benchmark built from Thai exam questions. Published evaluations found GPT-4-class systems at roughly 40% accuracy, while most other models scored substantially lower, indicating that it remains much harder than English-language MMLU.

guess: JMedQA (Japanese Medical QA), a JMLE-derived benchmark
known_results: In published evaluations, GPT-4/4o and Claude-class models generally perform best, while open-weight Japanese models trail considerably. Even leading systems remain below expert-level reliability, with image-based questions tending to be harder.

KMMLU is a Korean four-way multiple-choice knowledge benchmark spanning six broad domains, with chance accuracy at 25%. Published comparisons place GPT-4 among the strongest systems at roughly the low-70% accuracy range, while most smaller and open models score substantially lower.

OlympiadBench uses challenging problems collected from national and international mathematics olympiads. In its original evaluation, strong AI systems generally achieved only tens-of-percent accuracy overall, with proof-based problems scoring substantially lower than answer-only questions.

guess: EHRSQL (EHR text-to-SQL benchmark, incl. its 2024 extension with eICU)
known_results: EHRSQL is an execution-accuracy benchmark for translating clinical questions into SQL over EHR databases (MIMIC-III in the original release, with eICU-style schemas and unanswerable questions in the later extension, where the gold output is an empty string). Reported results show zero-shot proprietary LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) scoring only moderate-to-low execution accuracy, while purpose-built/fine-tuned seq2seq models reach roughly 80-90%, with question rewriting/calibration methods proposed to improve reliability on unanswerable cases.

These examples appear to come from BIG-bench's auto_categorization task. In the original BIG-bench report, PaLM 540B led the full benchmark with roughly 69% normalized score, while GPT-3 175B scored in the high 40s; modern instruction-tuned models are considerably stronger on many individual tasks.

The English/USMLE split of MedQA is a standard medical multiple-choice benchmark. Med-PaLM 2 achieved about 86.5% accuracy, while strong large language models generally score in the mid-80% range or higher and smaller models score substantially lower.

Med-HALT is a binary benchmark for detecting hallucinations in medical question-answer pairs using categories such as misinterpretation, incompleteness, and biological mechanism misattribution. Published evaluations found that stronger models generally performed better, but even leading systems made substantial errors and did not achieve fully reliable hallucination detection.

guess: PathMMU: A Massive Multimodal Expert-Level Benchmark for Understanding and Reasoning in Pathology
known_results: PathMMU is intentionally difficult: evaluations have shown that even strong proprietary multimodal models generally achieve only around 40–50% accuracy, while most open or pathology-specific systems score lower and all remain well below expert-level performance.

AIRBench is Perplexity AI's roughly 5,000-example A/B safety-classification benchmark covering adversarial prompts, hallucinations, toxic language, and bias. Published leaderboards generally place GPT-4o- and Claude 3.5-class frontier models near the top, with older, smaller, and open models trailing; results vary considerably by risk category.

guess: MIR (Médico Interno Residente / Spanish Medical Internal Resident exam)
known_results: It consists of Spanish-language, five-option questions from Spain’s MIR residency entrance exam and has also been evaluated within MultiMedQA. Published evaluations place leading medical or GPT-4-class systems roughly in the 70–80% range, compared with a 20% random baseline, while earlier and smaller models generally score substantially lower.

PlanBench found GPT-4 to be the strongest evaluated model, but its plan-generation success rate was only about 64% overall and fell sharply on harder, larger instances; other LLMs generally performed substantially worse.

AssistantBench (a DeepMind/Google benchmark of realistic, casually phrased multi-site web tasks, e.g., shopping, hotel/local search, and ride-hailing across simulated sites such as the 'Omnizon' store) reports that even strong browser-agent setups solve only a minority of scenarios (roughly 20-30% success), far below human performance.

Winoground (Krishna et al., 2022) contains 400 minimal-pair examples with 800 images and captions differing by a small visual detail. Human accuracy was roughly 85–90%, while many zero-shot vision-language models performed near chance at around 50%.

This benchmark evaluates models on more than 1,600 crowd-sourced tasks specified through natural-language instructions and examples. Published evaluations found that instruction-tuned, multitask models generally outperform base models on held-out tasks, while performance varies substantially by task and often improves with more demonstrations.

This benchmark contains 2,438 repository-level issue-fixing tasks across nine programming languages. In published evaluations, strong Claude/GPT-based agents generally resolved only a minority of instances—often around 20–40%—while many simpler baselines scored near or below 10%.

Terminal-Bench 2.0 is Laude Institute's benchmark of difficult, real-world terminal, desktop, and system-administration tasks. Published leaderboards generally show frontier agents solving only a minority of tasks—typically a few tens of percent and far below human task experts—though results vary substantially by model and agent scaffold.

M3Exam is a multilingual, multi-subject exam benchmark containing text and image multiple-choice questions. Published evaluations show frontier proprietary models generally leading while most open models trail, with substantial variation by language and subject and meaningful headroom even for the strongest systems.

WorkBench is a multi-application workplace-agent benchmark covering calendar, project-management, and data-analysis tasks. Published evaluations found that LLM-based agents achieved only moderate task-success rates, with frequent multi-step and state-tracking errors, and generally trailed human experts.

In the original Perception Test paper, the best model achieved about 46.4% accuracy versus about 95.3% for humans. Later multimodal video models have improved substantially, but sound-conditioned visual questions remain challenging.

LiveBench is a continually refreshed, contamination-resistant LLM benchmark whose math items often use invertible transformations of competition problems. At launch, o1-preview led with an overall score of roughly 66%, while other leading models were generally in the 40–55% range; math and coding were among the harder categories.

FLAME reports that GPT-4 and other strong proprietary models generally achieved the best overall scores, while results varied by task and smaller or finance-specialized models remained competitive on narrower classification tasks such as FOMC.
